If that is not possible, the ladder must be secured at its top to a rigid support and a grasping device provided (1926.1053(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: the extension ladder to the roof sticks up 3 feet past the eave.

test.question: What inspection does 1926.1053(b)(15) require for ladders?
options: Inspection by a competent person for visible defects periodically and after any occurrence that could affect safe use
Monthly inspection by the manufacturer
Weekly inspection by the owner
An annual third-party inspection
test.explanation: Ladders must be inspected by a competent person for visible defects on a periodic basis and after any occurrence that could affect their safe use (1926.1053(b)(15)). Checking before each use is good practice, but the standard sets the competent-person inspection. Job-site scenario: after a stepladder is knocked over by a forklift, the competent person inspects it before reuse.

test.question: Under 1926.1053(a)(1), a portable ladder must be able to support at least how much without failure?
options: 300 pounds
Four times the maximum intended load (3.3 times for extra-heavy-duty type 1A metal or plastic ladders)
Three times the maximum intended load (2.5 times for extra-heavy-duty type 1A metal or reinforced plastic ladders)
Twice the combined weight of the worker, tools, and materials, or 300 pounds for type I ladders, whichever is greater
test.explanation: Self-supporting and non-self-supporting portable ladders must support at least four times the maximum intended load, except extra-heavy-duty type 1A metal or plastic ladders, which must sustain at least 3.3 times (1926.1053(a)(1)(i)-(ii)). Ladders may not be loaded beyond their maximum intended load or rated capacity (1926.1053(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: pick a ladder whose rating covers the worker plus tools and materials.

test.question: A ladder is found with a split side rail. What does 1926.1053(b)(16) require?
options: Keep using it until the end of the job
Wrap the rail with tape
Mark it as defective or tag it "Do Not Use", and withdraw it from service until repaired
Supervisor decides
test.explanation: Portable ladders with structural defects such as broken or split rails must be immediately marked as defective or tagged "Do Not Use" (or similar) and withdrawn from service until repaired (1926.1053(b)(16)). Repairs must restore the original design criteria (1926.1053(b)(18)). Job-site scenario: the split ladder is tagged and removed from the job.

test.question: Under 1926.1053(b)(6), on what surfaces may ladders be used?
options: Concrete only
On any surface, provided the ladder has slip-resistant feet and is set at the proper 4:1 angle
Only indoors
Only on stable and level surfaces, unless secured to prevent accidental displacement
test.explanation: Ladders may be used only on stable and level surfaces unless secured against accidental displacement (1926.1053(b)(6)). On slippery surfaces they must be secured or have slip-resistant feet (1926.1053(b)(7)). Job-site scenario: on soft soil, set the ladder on a firm, level base and secure it.

test.question: What does 1926.1053(b)(22) say about carrying items on a ladder?
options: An employee may not carry any object or load that could cause them to lose balance and fall
Loads up to 50 pounds may be carried, as long as the worker faces the ladder and keeps one hand on a rail
Any object may be carried if the worker keeps three points of contact, counting the hand holding the object as one
Items may be carried in either hand as long as the ladder is tied off at the top and a coworker holds the base
test.explanation: An employee may not carry any object or load that could cause them to lose balance and fall (1926.1053(b)(22)). At least one hand must grasp the ladder while climbing (1926.1053(b)(21)), and the user must face the ladder (1926.1053(b)(20)). Job-site scenario: the electrician uses a tool belt and hoists the conduit bundle up by hand line.

test.question: A ladder is set up in a doorway where foot traffic could knock it. What does 1926.1053(b)(8) require?
options: Set it at a 4:1 angle with slip-resistant feet and post a warning sign on both sides of the doorway
Secure the ladder to prevent accidental displacement, or barricade to keep traffic away
Tie it off only if it is over 20 feet long; shorter ladders just need a caution sign on the door
Post a sign only
test.explanation: Ladders placed where workplace activities or traffic could displace them, such as passageways, doorways, or driveways, must be secured or barricaded (1926.1053(b)(8)). Job-site scenario: cones and caution tape route traffic around a ladder in a corridor door.

test.question: Under 1926.1053(b)(12), what kind of ladder is required where the employee or ladder could contact exposed energized electrical equipment?
options: Any ladder, used carefully
An aluminum ladder with rubber feet
A ladder with nonconductive siderails
A wooden ladder painted with opaque coating
test.explanation: Ladders must have nonconductive siderails if used where the employee or ladder could contact exposed energized electrical equipment, except as provided in 1926.955 (1926.1053(b)(12)). Wood ladders may not be coated with an opaque covering (1926.1053(a)(12)). Job-site scenario: a fiberglass stepladder is used to work near an open panel.

test.question: What does 1926.1053(b)(13) say about the top of a stepladder?
options: It may be used if someone holds the ladder
Standing on it is fine for short tasks
The second step from the top is also prohibited
The top or top step may not be used as a step
test.explanation: The top or top step of a stepladder may not be used as a step (1926.1053(b)(13)). The "two steps down" rule is manufacturer and ANSI labeling, not 1926 text. Job-site scenario: if the painter needs the top step to reach, get a taller ladder.

test.question: Where platforms are overlapped to make a longer platform, what does 1926.451(b)(7) require?
options: The overlap must occur only over supports and be at least 12 inches, unless the platforms are nailed together or otherwise restrained
The overlap must be at least 6 inches anywhere
The overlap must be 18 inches between supports
No overlap is needed if cleated
test.explanation: Overlaps must occur only over supports and be at least 12 inches, unless the platforms are nailed together or otherwise restrained (1926.451(b)(7)). Separately, each platform end must extend over the centerline of its support by at least 6 inches unless cleated or restrained (1926.451(b)(4)). Job-site scenario: two planks overlap 12 inches directly over a frame bearer.

test.question: Who must inspect scaffolds before each work shift under 1926.451(f)(3)?
options: Each worker using the scaffold
A competent person
The supervisor
The safety manager
test.explanation: Scaffolds and components must be inspected for visible defects by a competent person before each work shift and after any occurrence that could affect structural integrity (1926.451(f)(3)). Job-site scenario: the designated competent person tags the scaffold green after the morning inspection.

test.question: Under 1926.451(f)(7), scaffolds may be erected, moved, dismantled, or altered only:
options: By any available laborers, provided the site superintendent reviews the manufacturer's erection instructions with them and inspects the scaffold before first use
After a registered engineer stamps the erection drawings, by any crew that has read the manufacturer's instructions, with the foreman signing off at the end
Under the supervision and direction of a competent person qualified in those activities, by experienced and trained employees selected for the work
On weekends
test.explanation: Erecting, moving, dismantling, or altering scaffolds must be done only under the supervision and direction of a qualified competent person, by experienced and trained employees selected by that competent person (1926.451(f)(7)). Job-site scenario: the scaffold foreman directs a trained crew when adding a lift.

test.question: When there is a danger of tools or materials falling from a scaffold onto employees below, which does 1926.451(h)(2) require?
options: Hard hats for workers below plus a toeboard at least 2 inches high on edges over 20 feet up; barricading cannot replace the toeboard, and canopies, debris nets, or catch platforms are allowed for suspended scaffolds only
Only hard hats for workers below
Warning signs posted below in place of a barricade

One listed measure, such as barricading the area below to keep employees out, a toeboard on edges over 10 feet up, guardrails with openings too small for objects to pass, or a canopy, debris net, or catch platform
test.explanation: Where objects could fall and strike employees below, either barricade the area below and keep employees out (1926.451(h)(2)(i)), or install a toeboard along platform edges more than 10 feet above lower levels (1926.451(h)(2)(ii)). Other listed measures include paneling or screening where materials are piled above the toeboard (1926.451(h)(2)(iii)), a guardrail system with openings small enough to prevent passage of falling objects (1926.451(h)(2)(iv)), or a canopy, debris net, or catch platform (1926.451(h)(2)(v)). Toeboards must be at least 3.5 inches high and withstand 50 pounds (1926.451(h)(4)). Job-site scenario: masons 14 feet up get toeboards because the sidewalk below stays open.

test.question: Under 1926.451(b)(3), how far may the front edge of a platform be from the face of the work unless guardrails or personal fall arrest are used?
options: 16 inches for masonry work
14 inches
18 inches
20 inches with toeboards
test.explanation: The front edge of platforms may not be more than 14 inches from the face of the work unless guardrails are erected along the front edge and/or personal fall arrest systems are used, with listed exceptions (1926.451(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: bricklayers keep the platform within 14 inches of the wall.

test.question: How often must suspension scaffold ropes be inspected under 1926.451(d)(10)?
options: Weekly by the scaffold operator, plus a check by the manufacturer's representative whenever a rope is replaced or re-reeved
By a competent person prior to each workshift and after every occurrence that could affect the rope's integrity
Monthly by a qualified rigger, with any rope showing broken wires tagged and replaced at the next scheduled rope change
Annually
test.explanation: Ropes must be inspected for defects by a competent person before each workshift and after every occurrence that could affect their integrity, and replaced if listed conditions exist (1926.451(d)(10)). Job-site scenario: the window-washing crew's competent person checks the ropes for broken wires each morning.

test.question: Where must the bottom rung of a hook-on or attachable scaffold ladder be positioned under 1926.451(e)(2)(ii)?
options: No more than 36 inches above grade
Touching the ground
No more than 24 inches above the scaffold supporting level
Anywhere convenient
test.explanation: Hook-on and attachable ladders must be positioned so their bottom rung is no more than 24 inches above the scaffold supporting level (1926.451(e)(2)(ii)). Ladders or other listed access are required when platforms are more than 2 feet above or below the access point (1926.451(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: after grading, the attachable ladder is extended so the first rung is within 24 inches of the ground.

test.question: How must fabricated frame scaffolds be braced under 1926.452(c)(2)?
options: With braces hooked on but left unpinned
Only the end sections
Only above 20 feet
By cross, horizontal, or diagonal braces (or a combination) that secure vertical members together laterally, with all brace connections secured
test.explanation: Frames and panels must be braced by cross, horizontal, or diagonal braces, or a combination, that secure vertical members together laterally and keep the scaffold plumb, level, and square. All brace connections must be secured (1926.452(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: every frame set gets its cross braces pinned before planking.

test.question: What load must each suspension rope on a non-adjustable suspension scaffold support under 1926.451(a)(3)?
options: 4 times the maximum intended load
6 times the maximum intended load
8 times the maximum intended load
10 times the maximum intended load
test.explanation: Each suspension rope and its connecting hardware must support at least 6 times the maximum intended load (1926.451(a)(3)). Adjustable suspension scaffolds also require 6 times, calculated at the greater of the hoist's rated load or twice its stall load (1926.451(a)(4)). Job-site scenario: rigging for a two-point swing stage is checked against the 6:1 requirement.

test.question: A scaffold frame member is bent. What does 1926.451(f)(4) require?
options: Keep using it if the bend is minor, with a note in the inspection log so the competent person can review it at the next weekly check
Immediately repair, replace, or brace it to meet capacity requirements, or remove it from service until repaired
Mark it with red paint and keep it in service at full load until the scaffold supplier picks it up for repair at the end of the month
Get written approval from a registered professional engineer before the next shift; until it arrives, the platform above the bent frame may be used for material storage only
test.explanation: Any scaffold part damaged or weakened below the required strength must be immediately repaired or replaced, braced to meet the capacity provisions, or removed from service until repaired (1926.451(f)(4)). Job-site scenario: the bent frame is swapped out before work resumes.

title: Steel Erection Safety
topics: Fall protection triggers for steel erection and connectors

resources.title: Steel Erection Fall Protection
resources.description: Fall protection for steel erection, connectors, and controlled decking zones

test.question: Under 1926.760(b)(1), connectors must be protected from fall hazards of more than:
options: 15 feet
30 feet only
Two stories or 30 feet above a lower level, whichever is less
Three stories
test.explanation: Connectors must be protected from fall hazards of more than two stories or 30 feet above a lower level, whichever is less (1926.760(b)(1)). At heights over 15 and up to 30 feet, they must be provided with a personal fall arrest, positioning, or restraint system and wear the equipment needed to tie off, or be provided with other fall protection meeting (a)(1) (1926.760(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: on a building with 12-foot stories, a connector at 25 feet (above two stories) must be protected.

test.question: Before steel erection begins, what does 1926.752(b) require the steel erector to have received?
options: Verbal notice from the concrete contractor that the footings, piers, and walls have cured at least 7 days and reached 50% of the intended design strength before the first columns are set
A building permit and a stamped foundation plan showing the design strength of the footings, piers, and walls, which the erector may rely on without any strength test of the placed concrete
A team meeting sign-in sheet showing the crew was told the footings and piers had cured at least 28 days since placement, which the erector may accept in place of strength test results
Written notification that the concrete in footings, piers, and walls (or masonry mortar) has reached 75% of design strength or enough strength to support erection loads
test.explanation: A steel erector may not erect steel without written notification that the concrete or mortar has reached, based on an appropriate ASTM test of field-cured samples, 75% of the intended minimum compressive design strength or enough strength to support the loads imposed during erection (1926.752(b)). The controlling contractor provides it (1926.752(a)). Job-site scenario: the GC hands the erector the test report and written approval before the first column is set.

test.question: Under 1926.760(a)(1), above what height must an employee doing steel erection (other than connectors and CDZ workers) be protected at an unprotected side or edge?
options: 6 feet
10 feet
15 feet
30 feet
test.explanation: Each employee in steel erection on a surface with an unprotected side or edge more than 15 feet above a lower level must be protected by guardrails, safety nets, personal fall arrest, positioning device, or fall restraint systems. Connectors and controlled decking zone workers are covered separately (1926.760(a)(1), (a)(3)). Job-site scenario: a welder on an 18-foot beam ties off.

test.question: Under 1926.753(e)(1)(i), what must be used to perform a multiple lift?
options: A choker sling rated for the total weight of the members
A multiple lift rigging assembly
Standard alloy chains choked around each member
Rope only
test.explanation: A multiple lift may be performed only if a multiple lift rigging assembly is used, among other criteria (1926.753(e)(1)(i)). Employees doing multiple lift rigging need special training (1926.761(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: the raising gang uses a purpose-built multiple lift assembly for the beam pick.

test.question: When is a site-specific erection plan required under 1926.752(e)?
options: Always
Only above 5 stories
When the employer chooses, because of site conditions, to use alternate means and methods allowed by 1926.753(c)(5), 1926.757(a)(4), or 1926.757(e)(4); it must be developed by a qualified person
Whenever a crane is used to hoist steel
test.explanation: Where the employer elects alternate means and methods under the listed paragraphs because of site-specific conditions, a site-specific erection plan must be developed by a qualified person and be available at the work site (1926.752(e)). Job-site scenario: the erector wants to deactivate hook safety latches while placing purlins, so a qualified person writes a site-specific erection plan providing equivalent protection (1926.753(c)(5)(ii)).

test.question: What is the maximum number of members that may be hoisted in one multiple lift under 1926.753(e)(1)(ii)?
test.explanation: A maximum of five members may be hoisted per lift, and only beams and similar structural members may be lifted (1926.753(e)(1)(ii)-(iii)). Job-site scenario: a christmas-tree lift of five beams is the limit.

test.question: Under 1926.754(e)(5)(i), when must metal decking be secured (outside a controlled decking zone)?
options: Laid tightly and immediately secured upon placement
Laid loosely and secured at the end of each shift or before high winds
At the end of the week
Only when wind is forecast, with bundles banded until then
test.explanation: Except in a controlled decking zone under 1926.760(c), metal decking must be laid tightly and immediately secured upon placement (1926.754(e)(5)(i)). Bundles must also be secured at the end of the shift or when conditions require (1926.754(e)(1)(v)). Job-site scenario: each sheet is tack-welded or screwed as it is placed.

test.question: During steel erection, how may a crane hoist employees under 1926.753(c)(4)?
options: On the hook or headache ball, riding a choker loop, if each worker wears a harness tied to the hoist line
On a personnel platform, provided all provisions of 1926.1431 (except 1926.1431(a)) are met
On a load of steel
In a material box or bucket lifted by the crane, if workers are tied off to the box with personal fall arrest
test.explanation: Cranes or derricks may hoist employees on a personnel platform during steel erection, provided all provisions of 1926.1431 except 1926.1431(a) are met (1926.753(c)(4)). Job-site scenario: bolt-up crews ride a certified personnel platform rigged per 1926.1431, never the hook.

test.question: Under 1926.753(d)(1), which employees may work directly below a suspended load during steel erection?
options: Anyone wearing a hard hat
Only the foreman
Only employees engaged in the initial connection of the steel, or those needed to hook or unhook the load
Any member of the raising gang, as long as the load is rigged with a tag line and the operator sounds the horn first
test.explanation: Routes for suspended loads must be pre-planned so no employee works directly below a suspended load, except employees engaged in the initial connection of the steel or those needed to hook or unhook the load (1926.753(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: the decking crew moves aside while the beam swings over.

test.question: Under 1926.761(a), who must provide the training required by the steel erection standard?
options: Any experienced ironworker
The crane operator
OSHA
A qualified person
test.explanation: Training required by 1926.761 must be provided by a qualified person (1926.761(a)). Each employee exposed to a fall hazard must be trained in recognizing hazards and using fall protection systems (1926.761(b)). Job-site scenario: a qualified trainer delivers the connector and decking training before the raising gang starts.

title: Electrical Safety Fundamentals
topics: GFCI or assured equipment grounding program

resources.title: Ground Fault Protection
resources.description: GFCI and assured equipment grounding conductor program requirements

resources.title: Electrical Safety-Related Work Practices
resources.description: Protection of employees from energized circuits

test.question: Under 1926.404(b)(1)(ii), which receptacles need GFCI protection if the employer uses the GFCI option?
options: All 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-amp receptacles on construction sites that are not part of the building's permanent wiring and are in use by employees
Only those in wet locations
Every circuit of any voltage
Only receptacles on generators
test.explanation: The employer must use either GFCIs or an assured equipment grounding conductor program (1926.404(b)(1)(i)). Under the GFCI option, all 120-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-amp receptacles not part of the permanent wiring and in use by employees need GFCIs. Receptacles on two-wire, single-phase portable or vehicle-mounted generators rated 5 kW or less, with conductors insulated from the frame and other grounded surfaces, are exempt (1926.404(b)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: every temporary-power outlet on the spider box is GFCI-protected.

test.question: Under 1926.416(a)(1), when may an employee work close enough to contact part of an electric power circuit?
options: Whenever the circuit's breaker has been switched off and tagged at the panel, even though the conductors have not been grounded or guarded by insulation or other means
Only when protected against electric shock by deenergizing and grounding the circuit, or by guarding it effectively with insulation or other means
Whenever the employee wears leather work gloves and uses tools with plastic-coated handles, with a second electrician standing by to cut power if contact occurs
Whenever the circuit operates at 50 volts or less
test.explanation: No employee may work in proximity to any part of an electric power circuit they could contact unless protected by deenergizing and grounding the circuit or by guarding it effectively with insulation or other means (1926.416(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: before pulling wire near a live bus, the circuit is deenergized and grounded, or the bus is covered with insulating blankets.

test.question: Under an assured equipment grounding conductor program, when must the required tests be performed (1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(E))?
options: Before first use, after any repairs, after any incident suspected of causing damage, and at intervals not exceeding 6 months (12 months for fixed cord sets and for receptacles not exposed to damage)
Annually
Before first use, after repairs, after any incident suspected of causing damage, and at intervals not exceeding 3 months (6 months for fixed cord sets and receptacles not exposed to damage)
Only when a GFCI trips
test.explanation: Tests are required before first use, before return to service after repairs, before use after a suspected-damage incident, and at least every 3 months (6 months for fixed cord sets and receptacles not exposed to damage) (1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(E)). Cords and equipment must also be visually inspected before each day's use (1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(C)), and tests must be recorded (1926.404(b)(1)(iii)(G)). Job-site scenario: a cord run over by a skid steer is retested before reuse.

test.question: What does 1926.404(a)(1) require of an equipment grounding conductor?
options: It must be green
It must be the largest conductor
It may match the grounded conductor's color
It must be identifiable and distinguishable from all other conductors
test.explanation: A conductor used as an equipment grounding conductor must be identifiable and distinguishable from all other conductors (1926.404(a)(1)). Green (or bare) is the common electrical-code convention, but that color is not stated in 1926 text. Job-site scenario: the electrician confirms the cord's grounding conductor goes to the grounding terminal and polarity is not reversed (1926.404(a)(2)).

test.question: Under 1926.416(d), what must be used when fuses are installed or removed with one or both terminals energized?
options: Special tools insulated for the voltage
Bare hands with dry gloves
A standard screwdriver with a plastic handle
Pliers with electrical tape wrapped around both handles
test.explanation: When fuses are installed or removed with one or both terminals energized, special tools insulated for the voltage must be used (1926.416(d)). Job-site scenario: the electrician uses a rated fuse puller on the live disconnect.

test.question: What does 1926.405(a)(2)(ii)(E) require for temporary lighting?
options: Temporary lights must use 12-volt lamps throughout the site, and metal-case sockets may be left ungrounded if the lamps have wire cages
Lamps for general illumination must be protected from accidental contact or breakage, and metal-case sockets must be grounded
Lamps must be mounted at least 7 feet above the working surface, and temporary light strings may be hung by their own electric cords between supports
Daily replacement
test.explanation: All lamps for general illumination must be protected from accidental contact or breakage, and metal-case sockets must be grounded (1926.405(a)(2)(ii)(E)). Job-site scenario: temporary string lights in the stairwell have cage guards on every bulb.

test.question: How must flexible cords be protected on a job site?
options: Run them through doorways and pinch points without added protection
Cords may be fastened to framing with insulated staples or hung from nails along the wall, as long as worn or frayed sections are taped first
They must be protected from damage, and extension cords may not be fastened with staples, hung from nails, or suspended by wire
Only marked with paint
test.explanation: Flexible cords and cables must be protected from damage, avoiding sharp corners and projections (1926.405(a)(2)(ii)(I)). Extension cords may not be stapled, hung from nails, or suspended by wire (1926.416(e)(2)), and worn or frayed cords may not be used (1926.416(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: cords crossing a doorway are run through a cord protector, not nailed to the frame.

test.question: A 120/208-volt panel (150 volts or less to ground) has exposed live parts on one side and no live or grounded parts on the other. What is the minimum working clearance in front of it under Table K-1 of 1926.403(i)(1)(i)?
options: 2 1/2 feet (30 inches)
2 feet
3 feet
3 1/2 feet
test.explanation: For 0-150 volts to ground, Table K-1 requires 3 feet for conditions (a), (b), and (c). For 151-600 volts, it requires 3, 3.5, or 4 feet depending on the condition. Workspace must also be at least 30 inches wide (1926.403(i)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: keep 3 feet clear in front of the temporary panel; no material staging there.

test.question: Before work begins, what does 1926.416(a)(3) require the employer to determine?
options: Whether any part of an energized power circuit, exposed or concealed, could be contacted by a person, tool, or machine during the work, with warning signs posted and employees advised
Whether any exposed energized circuit lies within 10 feet of the planned work, using the building drawings only; concealed circuits in walls or slabs are checked by electricians as they cut into them
Only the location of the main panel
The utility account number
test.explanation: Before work begins, the employer must find out by inquiry, direct observation, or instruments whether any energized circuit, exposed or concealed, could be contacted during the work. Where one exists, the employer must post and maintain warning signs and advise employees (1926.416(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: before core drilling a wall, check drawings and scan for live conduits.

test.question: Workers will use jackhammers where the exact location of underground power lines is unknown. What does 1926.416(a)(2) require?
options: A utility locate before digging, with no added PPE for hand tool users
Insulated protective gloves for employees using jackhammers, bars, or other hand tools that may contact a line
Only a face shield
Rubber boots only
test.explanation: Where the exact location of underground electric powerlines is unknown, employees using jackhammers, bars, or other hand tools that may contact a line must be given insulated protective gloves (1926.416(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: the crew breaking a slab over an unknown duct bank wears rated insulating gloves.

title: Lockout and Tagging of Circuits (Construction)
topics: Rendering deenergized circuits inoperative and tagging every energizing point
Locating energized circuits and posting warnings

resources.title: Lockout and Tagging of Circuits
resources.description: Construction requirements for tagging controls and deenergized circuits

resources.title: Electrical Safety-Related Work Practices
resources.description: Protection from energized circuits during construction

resources.title: LOTO eTool
resources.description: Interactive LOTO training. The full energy control program (written procedures, periodic inspection, training certification) is covered in the 1910 track, Week 2 (29 CFR 1910.147).

test.question: Under 1926.417(a), what must be done to controls that are to be deactivated while work is done on energized or deenergized equipment or circuits?
options: They must be locked, with no tag needed
They must be removed
They must be tagged
They must be painted red
test.explanation: Controls that are to be deactivated during work on energized or deenergized equipment or circuits must be tagged (1926.417(a)). Job-site scenario: the motor starter switched off for conduit work gets a tag before the crew starts. (1910.147 is the general-industry lockout standard; it does not cover construction work (1910.147(a)(1)(ii)(A)) and is covered in 1910 Week 2.)

test.question: Under 1926.417(b), what is required for equipment or circuits that are deenergized?
options: A sign at the main panel only
A verbal warning to the crew
Switched off, with the panel door closed
They must be rendered inoperative and have tags attached at all points where they can be energized
test.explanation: Deenergized equipment or circuits must be rendered inoperative and have tags attached at all points where they can be energized (1926.417(b)). Job-site scenario: a feeder that can be energized from two panels is made inoperative and tagged at both.

test.question: Under 1926.417(c), how must tags be placed?
options: To identify plainly the equipment or circuits being worked on
Anywhere on the panel door
On the main disconnect only, since one tag there covers every downstream circuit
On the worker's hard hat or clothing, so the tag stays with the person doing the work
test.explanation: Tags must be placed to plainly identify the equipment or circuits being worked on (1926.417(c)). Job-site scenario: the tag on breaker 14 reads "Panel LP-2, circuit 14, lighting Level 3 - men working."

test.question: Under 1926.416(a)(1), how must an employee be protected before working where they could contact part of an electric power circuit?
options: By posting and maintaining warning signs at the circuit and advising the employee of its location and the hazards involved
By deenergizing the circuit and grounding it, or by guarding it effectively with insulation or other means
By a visual check only
By wearing a hard hat
test.explanation: An employee may not work where they could contact any part of an electric power circuit unless protected by deenergizing and grounding it, or by guarding it effectively by insulation or other means (1926.416(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: after tagging the circuit, the electrician tests it dead and applies grounds before working on the conductors.

test.question: Under 1926.416(a)(3), what must the employer do before work begins near possibly energized circuits?
options: Rely on the drawings only
Only notify the utility
Find out by inquiry, observation, or instruments whether energized circuits could be contacted; post and maintain warning signs; and advise employees
Have the electrical foreman check for live circuits as the work proceeds, and post warning signs only after an employee reports contact or a shock from a concealed line
test.explanation: The employer must determine whether any part of an energized circuit, exposed or concealed, could be contacted during the work. Where one exists, it must post and maintain warning signs and advise employees of its location and hazards (1926.416(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: before demo of a ceiling, the crew locates live branch circuits and flags them.

test.question: Under 1926.416(d), what must be used to install or remove fuses when one or both terminals are energized?
options: Any tool
Gloves only
A wooden stick
Special tools insulated for the voltage
test.explanation: Fuses installed or removed with one or both terminals energized require special tools insulated for the voltage (1926.416(d)). Job-site scenario: an insulated fuse puller is used on the energized switch.

test.question: Under 1926.416(b)(1), what must be provided when energized parts of electrical equipment are exposed?
options: Barriers or other guarding so the workspace is not used as a passageway
A warning sign on the open panel, with the workspace kept open as a walkway for other trades
Extra task lighting and a second qualified electrician standing by at the open panel
A second electrician
test.explanation: Barriers or other guarding must keep the workspace for electrical equipment from being used as a passageway while energized parts are exposed (1926.416(b)(1)). Working spaces and walkways must be kept clear of cords (1926.416(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: caution tape and stanchions close the corridor in front of the open switchboard.

test.question: In an existing installation, what does 1926.416(c) prohibit?
options: Replacing a breaker with one of the same or lower ampere rating than the load rating of the existing circuit wiring
Changing circuit protection to increase the load beyond the load rating of the circuit wiring
Adding GFCIs
Labeling circuits
test.explanation: In existing installations, no change in circuit protection may be made to increase the load beyond the load rating of the circuit wiring (1926.416(c)). Job-site scenario: a 15-amp breaker on 14-gauge wire is not swapped for a 30-amp to stop nuisance trips.

test.question: A crew finds a frayed extension cord on the job. Under 1926.416(e)(1), what is required?
options: Tape it and keep using it
Use it only outdoors
Worn or frayed cords may not be used
Use it only at 120 volts
test.explanation: Worn or frayed electric cords or cables may not be used (1926.416(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: the frayed cord is tagged out and removed (see also 1926.20(b)(3)).

test.question: Under 1926.20(b)(3), how may equipment that does not comply with Part 1926 be taken out of use?
options: It may stay in use until the end of the shift if the operator is warned of the defect and a supervisor watches its use
By verbally instructing the operator and the rest of the crew not to use it until a mechanic has inspected and repaired it
By painting it
By tagging it as unsafe or locking its controls so it cannot be operated, or by physically removing it
test.explanation: Noncompliant machinery, tools, materials, or equipment must be identified as unsafe by tagging or locking the controls to make them inoperable, or physically removed (1926.20(b)(3)). This is the general 1926 basis for locking out controls. Job-site scenario: a saw table with a broken guard has its disconnect locked and tagged.

title: Excavation Safety Basics
topics: Sloping in Type C soil and the default slope

test.question: Under 1926.652(a)(1), when is a protective system NOT required in an excavation?
options: When it is made entirely in stable rock, or is less than 5 feet deep and a competent person finds no indication of a potential cave-in
When the excavation is less than 8 feet deep
When work will take less than an hour
When the soil is dry
test.explanation: Each employee in an excavation must be protected from cave-ins by an adequate protective system, except in excavations made entirely in stable rock, or less than 5 feet deep where a competent person's examination shows no indication of a potential cave-in (1926.652(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: a 5.5-foot water-line trench needs a protective system.

test.question: When must a competent person inspect excavations under 1926.651(k)(1)?
options: At the start of each work week by a competent person, and again after every rainstorm, vibration event, or other hazard-increasing occurrence
Daily before work starts, as needed throughout the shift, and after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing occurrence
Only after rain
Only before the first entry each day, by the crew foreman, with no further checks needed during the shift or after a rainstorm
test.explanation: Daily inspections of excavations, adjacent areas, and protective systems must be made by a competent person before work starts and as needed throughout the shift, and after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing occurrence, when employee exposure can be reasonably anticipated (1926.651(k)(1)). Job-site scenario: after an overnight storm, the competent person inspects before anyone enters.

test.question: What is the maximum allowable slope for a simple slope excavation 20 feet or less deep in Type C soil (1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, B-1.3)?
test.explanation: All simple slope excavations 20 feet or less deep in Type C soil have a maximum allowable slope of 1 1/2:1 (horizontal:vertical) (1926 Subpart P Appendix B (B-1.3)). Job-site scenario: an 8-foot-deep cut in sandy Type C soil is laid back 12 feet horizontally on each side.

test.question: Which configurations does Appendix B (Figure B-1, B-1.3) show for excavations 20 feet or less deep in Type C soil?
options: A simple bench and a multiple bench, each at a maximum slope of 1 1/2:1 with bench heights no greater than 4 feet, plus a vertically sided lower portion supported 18 inches above the vertical side
Simple bench only, at 3/4:1
Unsupported vertical sides up to 3 1/2 feet
A simple slope at 1 1/2:1 maximum, and a vertically sided lower portion shielded or supported at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side, also at 1 1/2:1; no benching is shown
test.explanation: Appendix B requires sloping and benching configurations to follow Figure B-1 (1926 Subpart P Appendix B (c)(4)). For Type C soil, B-1.3 shows simple slope excavations at a maximum allowable slope of 1 1/2:1, and vertically sided lower portions that are shielded or supported at least 18 inches above the vertical side, also at 1 1/2:1. Benched configurations are shown for Type A (B-1.1) and Type B (B-1.2) only. Other sloped configurations for Type C must use the other options in 1926.652(b) (B-1.3, item 3). Job-site scenario: in sandy Type C soil, the crew lays the walls back at 1 1/2:1.

test.question: Under 1926.651(c)(2), trench excavations 4 feet or more deep must have a stairway, ladder, ramp, or other safe means of egress located so employees need no more than ___ of lateral travel.
options: 25 feet
50 feet
75 feet
100 feet
test.explanation: A safe means of egress must be in trenches 4 feet or more deep so employees travel no more than 25 feet laterally to reach it (1926.651(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: in a 100-foot trench, ladders are placed so no one is more than 25 feet from one.

test.question: How far from the edge of an excavation must spoil and equipment be kept under 1926.651(j)(2)?
options: 5 feet
At least 2 feet, or use retaining devices (or both)
10 feet
At least 18 inches
test.explanation: Employees must be protected from excavated material or equipment falling or rolling into the excavation by keeping it at least 2 feet from the edge, by retaining devices, or both (1926.651(j)(2)). Job-site scenario: the excavator places spoil at least 2 feet back from the trench lip.

test.question: Under 1926.651(g)(1)(i), when must the atmosphere be tested before employees enter an excavation?
options: Only after a gas odor is noticed in the trench
When the excavation is more than 5 feet deep and the oxygen level could fall below 16%, or a hazardous atmosphere has been confirmed by odor or visible vapor
When the excavation is more than 4 feet deep and an oxygen deficiency (below 19.5%) or hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably be expected
Only when the excavation qualifies as a permit-required confined space, and then for oxygen and combustibles after employees report odors, headaches, or dizziness
test.explanation: Where oxygen deficiency (below 19.5%) or a hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably be expected, such as near landfills or stored hazardous substances, the atmosphere must be tested before employees enter excavations more than 4 feet deep (1926.651(g)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: a trench next to an old fuel tank is tested before entry.

test.question: After soil is classified, conditions change after heavy rain. What does Appendix A to Subpart P require (1926 Subpart P Appendix A (c)(5))?
options: The original classification stands until the excavation is completed, unless a cave-in or visible soil movement occurs
Reclassify only at the next scheduled annual review, by the engineer who did the original soil tests
Reclassify only at project start
A competent person must evaluate the changes and reclassify the deposit as necessary
test.explanation: If the properties, factors, or conditions affecting a classification change in any way, a competent person must evaluate the changes and reclassify the deposit as necessary (1926 Subpart P Appendix A (c)(5)). Job-site scenario: after saturation, the Type B classification is downgraded to Type C and slopes are cut back.

test.question: If water removal equipment is used to control water in an excavation, what does 1926.651(h)(2) require?
options: The equipment and operations must be monitored by a competent person
Nothing further, as long as the pump discharge is directed away from the trench
Pumping only at night
The equipment must be checked once at startup by the pump supplier, with no further monitoring needed
test.explanation: Employees may not work in excavations with accumulated or accumulating water unless adequate precautions are taken (1926.651(h)(1)). If water removal equipment is used, a competent person must monitor it and its operation (1926.651(h)(2)). Job-site scenario: the competent person checks the sump pumps throughout the shift.

test.question: What does 1926.651(a) require for surface encumbrances, such as a sidewalk slab next to a planned trench?
options: They must be evaluated after the trench is opened, and removed or supported only if cracks or visible settling then appear in the slab
Those located so as to create a hazard must be removed or supported as necessary to safeguard employees
Leave them in place
Only mark them with paint
test.explanation: All surface encumbrances located so as to create a hazard must be removed or supported as necessary to safeguard employees (1926.651(a)). Job-site scenario: the sidewalk panel next to the trench line is saw-cut and removed before digging alongside it.
