Access to the written program, chemical list, and SDSs
Chemical list in the written program

resources.title: Chemical Inventory Requirement
resources.description: Written program and list of hazardous chemicals (applies to construction via 1926.59)

test.question: Which elements must appear on the label of a shipped container of a hazardous chemical under 1910.1200(f)(1)?
options: Product identifier, signal word, hazard statement(s), and pictogram(s), plus the date of manufacture and the distributor's emergency number; precautionary statements are optional
Product identifier, hazard statement(s), and the supplier's 24-hour emergency phone number only; signal words and pictograms are given on the SDS instead of the label
Product identifier, signal word, hazard statement(s), pictogram(s), precautionary statement(s), and the responsible party's name, U.S. address, and phone number
Optional information
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Shipped containers must carry the product identifier, signal word, hazard statements, pictograms, precautionary statements, and the name, U.S. address, and U.S. phone number of the responsible party (1910.1200(f)(1)). Job-site scenario: the paint thinner can shows the flame pictogram, "Danger," and hazard statements.

test.question: Under 1910.1200(g)(8), how must safety data sheets be kept?
options: In the main office for 30 years after last use, with a copy sent out to the job site only when an employee submits a written request to the corporate safety department
Only at company headquarters, where the safety manager can email a copy to the job site within one business day after an employee calls the office to request it
Only on request
In the workplace and readily accessible to employees in their work areas during each work shift (electronic access is fine if there are no barriers)
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. SDSs must be kept in the workplace and readily accessible during each shift to employees in their work areas. Electronic access is permitted if it creates no barriers to immediate access (1910.1200(g)(8)). Employees who travel between sites may have SDSs kept at the primary facility if information is immediately available in an emergency (1910.1200(g)(9)). Job-site scenario: the SDS binder is in the gang box, or the app works without a login.

test.question: When must HazCom training be given under 1910.1200(h)(1)?
options: At initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard employees have not been trained on is introduced into their work area
Within 90 days after initial assignment, and at the next annual refresher after a new chemical hazard is introduced into the work area
Monthly
Annually, on the anniversary of hire
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Training is required at the time of initial assignment and whenever a new chemical hazard is introduced into the work area (1910.1200(h)(1)). Job-site scenario: before the new epoxy coating system is used, the crew is trained on it.

test.question: Under 1910.1200(h)(2)(iii), employees must be informed of the location and availability of:
options: Only the container labels and the pictograms posted in the trailer; the written program and SDSs stay with the safety manager
The written hazard communication program, including the required list(s) of hazardous chemicals, and the SDSs
Only the SDSs
Only the supervisor's copy of the SDSs; the written program and the chemical list are kept by the safety department and need not be shown
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Employees must be informed of the location and availability of the written program, including the list(s) of hazardous chemicals, and the SDSs (1910.1200(h)(2)(iii)). Job-site scenario: the orientation shows where the HazCom binder and chemical list are kept in the trailer.

test.question: Under 1910.1200(d)(1), who must classify the hazards of chemicals?
options: Every employer that uses the chemical on site, which must classify each hazard itself even when the manufacturer's or importer's classification is already provided
The site safety committee, which reviews each product's SDS and assigns its own hazard classes and categories before the chemical can be used by any crew on the job
Chemical manufacturers and importers (employers need not classify unless they choose not to rely on the manufacturer's or importer's classification)
Each construction employer using the chemical, by sending a sample of every product to a lab for testing to determine its hazards before allowing employees to use it
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Chemical manufacturers and importers must evaluate and classify the chemicals they produce or import. Employers are not required to classify unless they choose not to rely on the manufacturer's or importer's classification (1910.1200(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: the contractor relies on the supplier's classification shown on the SDS.

test.question: A worker needs to choose gloves for a new solvent. Which SDS section has exposure controls and personal protection information under 1910.1200(g)(2)?
options: Section 2
Section 4
Section 8
Section 11
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. SDS Section 8 is "Exposure controls/personal protection" (1910.1200(g)(2)(viii)). Job-site scenario: the foreman checks Section 8 for the recommended glove material.

test.question: A worker fills a bucket from a labeled drum and uses it right away, emptying it before leaving. Under 1910.1200(f)(8), must the bucket be labeled?
options: No; portable containers filled from labeled containers for the immediate use of the employee who did the transfer are exempt
Yes, every container must always be labeled
Yes; any portable container must be labeled once it holds more than 5 gallons, even if only the employee who filled it uses it right away
Labeling is optional for all containers
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Workplace containers must generally be labeled (1910.1200(f)(6)), but portable containers filled from labeled containers and intended only for the immediate use of the employee who did the transfer are exempt (1910.1200(f)(8)). Job-site scenario: a cleaning solution bucket that will be used by others across shifts must be labeled.

test.question: What must the list of hazardous chemicals in the written program include under 1910.1200(e)(1)(i)?
options: Detailed quantities and storage locations
The hazardous chemicals known to be present, using a product identifier that is referenced on the appropriate SDS
Only purchase dates
Only chemicals stored in quantities over 55 gallons
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. The written program must include a list of hazardous chemicals known to be present, using a product identifier referenced on the appropriate SDS. The list may cover the whole workplace or individual work areas (1910.1200(e)(1)(i)). 1910.1200(e)(1)(i) does not require quantities or storage locations on the list. Job-site scenario: the site list names each product as it appears on its SDS.

test.question: On a multi-employer site, what must the written HazCom program also include under 1910.1200(e)(2)?
options: A clause that each subcontractor brings its own SDSs instead of being given access to the host employer's
An annual review date
Methods for giving other employers access to SDSs, informing them of precautionary measures, and informing them of the labeling system used
A list of every subcontractor's employees
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Employers whose chemicals may expose other employers' employees must include methods to give the other employers on-site access to SDSs, inform them of precautionary measures, and inform them of the labeling system (1910.1200(e)(2)). Job-site scenario: the GC's program explains how subs get SDSs for products stored in the shared conex.

test.question: Per 1910.1200 Appendix C (C.2.3.1), what must every GHS pictogram look like?
options: A diamond with a red symbol on a white background and a black frame
A yellow triangle with black text
A blue circle
A square set on a point, with a black hazard symbol on a white background and a red frame
test.explanation: Under 1926.59, construction hazard communication requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.1200. Pictograms must be a square set at a point, with a black hazard symbol on a white background and a red frame wide enough to be clearly visible (1910.1200 Appendix C (C.2.3.1)). Which symbol goes with which hazard (such as corrosion) is shown in Figure C.1, which is an image in the eCFR. Job-site scenario: the acid container label shows a red-bordered diamond pictogram.

resources.title: Fire Prevention
resources.description: Includes indoor storage and segregation of noncompatible materials

resources.title: Indoor Storage of Flammable Liquids
resources.description: Cabinet limits and indoor storage requirements

test.question: Under 1926.151(d)(3), how must noncompatible materials that may create a fire hazard be stored indoors?
options: Segregated by a barrier with a fire resistance of at least 1 hour
Together on the same shelf, as long as each container is labeled and kept closed
Behind a 30-minute fire-rated partition
Mixed in small amounts, with a few feet of open aisle between groups
test.explanation: Noncompatible materials that may create a fire hazard must be segregated by a barrier with a fire resistance of at least 1 hour (1926.151(d)(3)). In general storage, noncompatible materials must be segregated (1926.250(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: oxidizers are stored behind a rated partition, away from flammable liquids.

test.question: Under 1926.152(b)(3), how much Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquid may be stored in one storage cabinet?
options: 25 gallons
60 gallons
120 gallons
200 gallons
test.explanation: No more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2, and/or 3 flammable liquids, or 120 gallons of Category 4, may be stored in any one cabinet. No more than three cabinets may be in a single storage area (1926.152(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: once the cabinet holds 60 gallons of solvents, extra product goes to an inside storage room.

test.question: What does 1926.152(a)(1) require for handling flammable liquids in quantities of 5 gallons or less?
options: The original shipping container, for any amount up to 5 gallons
Open buckets
Approved safety cans or DOT-approved containers (except highly viscous liquids; 1 gallon or less may stay in the original container)
Glass jars
test.explanation: Only approved containers and portable tanks may be used to store and handle flammable liquids. Approved safety cans or DOT-approved containers must be used for 5 gallons or less, except for highly viscous liquids, and 1 gallon or less may stay in its original container (1926.152(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: gasoline for the saws is kept in a red approved safety can.

test.question: Under 1926.152(a)(2), where may flammable liquids NOT be stored?
options: In approved storage cabinets holding no more than 60 gallons of Category 1, 2, or 3 liquids
In outdoor piles of no more than 1,100 gallons, kept 5 feet apart and at least 20 feet from any building
In inside storage rooms
In areas used for exits, stairways, or normally used for the safe passage of people
test.explanation: Flammable liquids may not be stored in areas used for exits, stairways, or normally used for the safe passage of people (1926.152(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: fuel cans are moved out of the stair landing.

test.question: Under 1926.152(c)(1), outdoor storage of flammable liquid containers (60 gallons or less each) is limited to:
options: 1,100 gallons per pile, piles 5 feet apart, and no nearer than 20 feet to a building
500 gallons per pile, piles 3 feet apart, and no nearer than 10 feet to any building or trailer
No pile limit, as long as piles are 20 feet from buildings
2,200 gallons per pile, piles 10 feet apart, and no nearer than 10 feet to any building on the site
test.explanation: Outdoor storage of containers up to 60 gallons each may not exceed 1,100 gallons in any one pile, with 5-foot clearance between piles and at least 20 feet from a building (1926.152(c)(1)). A 12-foot-wide fire apparatus access way must be within 200 feet (1926.152(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: drums are staged in two piles 5 feet apart, 25 feet from the trailer.

test.question: Under 1926.152(e)(2), what is required when transferring Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquids between containers?
options: Transfer by air pressure on the container
The containers must be electrically interconnected (bonded)
A quick transfer
Only gloves
test.explanation: Transfer of Category 1, 2, or 3 flammable liquids from one container to another may be done only when the containers are electrically interconnected (bonded) (1926.152(e)(2)). Job-site scenario: a bonding wire connects the drum and the safety can before dispensing.

test.question: What does 1926.152(c)(3) require for outdoor flammable liquid storage areas?
options: A gravel surface with no grading or dikes
Grading to divert spills toward the nearest building drain, or a curb or earth dike at least 6 inches high with no drainage provisions
Grading to divert spills away from buildings, or a curb or earth dike at least 12 inches high with drainage provisions
A roof
test.explanation: The storage area must be graded to divert spills away from buildings or other exposures, or be surrounded by a curb or earth dike at least 12 inches high, with provisions for draining water or spills (1926.152(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: the fuel storage pad has a 12-inch berm and a drain valve.

test.question: Under 1926.152(d)(1), where must a portable fire extinguisher be placed for a room storing more than 60 gallons of flammable liquids?
options: Inside the room at the back
Within 100 feet
Anywhere on the floor
Outside the room, no more than 10 feet from the door, rated at least 20-B
test.explanation: At least one portable fire extinguisher rated at least 20-B must be outside, and no more than 10 feet from, the door of any room storing more than 60 gallons of flammable liquids (1926.152(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: a 20-B extinguisher hangs just outside the paint storage room door.

test.question: Under 1926.152(b)(2)(iii), how must flammable liquid storage cabinets be labeled?
options: Conspicuously, with "Flammable-Keep Away from Open Flames"
No label is needed
With the owner's name only
With "Danger - Flammable Liquids - No Smoking" in red letters on each door
test.explanation: Cabinets must be labeled in conspicuous lettering, "Flammable-Keep Away from Open Flames" (1926.152(b)(2)(iii)). Job-site scenario: a site-built plywood cabinet gets the required label before use.

test.question: Where the eyes or body may be exposed to injurious corrosive materials, what does 1926.50(g) require?
options: A first aid kit with eyewash bottles kept in the site trailer, to be carried to the work area by a coworker when an exposure occurs
Suitable facilities for quick drenching or flushing of the eyes and body within the work area for immediate emergency use
A phone number for poison control
An eyewash station in the main office building
test.explanation: Where the eyes or body may be exposed to injurious corrosive materials, suitable facilities for quick drenching or flushing must be provided within the work area for immediate emergency use (1926.50(g)). Job-site scenario: a portable eyewash station is set up next to the battery charging area.

resources.title: Respiratory Standards
resources.description: Respiratory protection standard (applies to construction via 1926.103)

resources.title: Medical Evaluation Requirements
resources.description: Medical evaluation before fit testing or respirator use

test.question: How often must an employee using a tight-fitting respirator be fit tested under 1910.134(f)(2)?
options: Only once
Monthly
Before initial use, whenever a different facepiece is used, and at least annually
Every five years
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Fit testing is required before initial use, whenever a different facepiece (size, style, model, or make) is used, and at least annually (1910.134(f)(2)). Job-site scenario: a laborer cutting concrete is re-fit tested every year on the same half-mask model.

test.question: Under 1910.134(e)(2)(i), how must the physician or other licensed health care professional (PLHCP) perform medical evaluations?
options: By a hands-on physical exam with spirometry for every employee, because a written questionnaire alone does not satisfy the rule
No evaluation is needed for half masks
By a supervisor's observation
Using a medical questionnaire, or an initial medical examination that obtains the same information
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. The employer must identify a PLHCP to perform medical evaluations using a medical questionnaire or an initial medical exam that obtains the same information (1910.134(e)(2)(i)). The evaluation must be done before fit testing or use (1910.134(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: new hires complete the Appendix C questionnaire, which a PLHCP reviews before fit testing.

test.question: When there is no end-of-service-life indicator for an organic vapor cartridge, what must the employer do under 1910.134(d)(3)(iii)(B)(2)?
options: Implement a change schedule based on objective information or data, described in the written program
Change cartridges when the wearer first smells or tastes the vapor, with that practice noted in the crew's toolbox talk records
Change them when breathing resistance increases noticeably, since rising resistance shows the vapor sorbent is used up
Change them annually
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Without an appropriate ESLI, the employer must implement a canister/cartridge change schedule based on objective information or data, and describe its basis in the written program (1910.134(d)(3)(iii)(B)(2)). Job-site scenario: the painting crew changes cartridges at the interval set by the manufacturer's service-life calculator.

test.question: What must the employer do before selecting a respirator under 1910.134(d)(1)(iii)?
options: Choose an N95 filtering facepiece for any dust or vapor task, then schedule air sampling within the first 30 days of use to confirm the respirator's protection is adequate
Identify and evaluate the respiratory hazards, including a reasonable estimate of exposures and the contaminant's chemical state and physical form
Let the worker choose
Choose by cost only
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. The employer must identify and evaluate workplace respiratory hazards, including a reasonable estimate of employee exposures and the contaminant's chemical state and physical form (1910.134(d)(1)(iii)). It must select a NIOSH-certified respirator (1910.134(d)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: silica monitoring results drive the choice between a half mask and a PAPR.

test.question: When must a user seal check be performed on a tight-fitting respirator under 1910.134(g)(1)(iii)?
options: Once at the start of each shift, with no further check needed if the respirator is removed and put back on during the shift
Weekly, during the toolbox safety meeting
Each time the respirator is put on
Monthly
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Employees must perform a user seal check each time they put on a tight-fitting respirator (1910.134(g)(1)(iii)). Job-site scenario: positive and negative pressure checks are done every time the mask is donned, including after breaks.

test.question: Under 1910.134(g)(1)(i)(A), what facial hair prohibits wearing a tight-fitting respirator?
options: Any facial hair at all
Only beards longer than 1 inch
Only facial hair that keeps the wearer from passing a fit test
Facial hair that comes between the sealing surface of the facepiece and the face, or that interferes with valve function
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Tight-fitting respirators may not be worn by employees with facial hair that comes between the sealing surface and the face or interferes with valve function (1910.134(g)(1)(i)(A)). A mustache that stays clear of the seal is not prohibited by this text. Job-site scenario: a worker with a full beard switches to a loose-fitting PAPR hood.

test.question: How must respirators shared by more than one employee be cleaned under 1910.134(h)(1)(ii)?
options: Cleaned and disinfected before being worn by a different individual
Weekly
Only when visibly dirty
Monthly
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Respirators issued to more than one employee must be cleaned and disinfected before being worn by different individuals (1910.134(h)(1)(ii)), using Appendix B-2 or equivalent manufacturer procedures (1910.134(h)(1)). Job-site scenario: the shared full-face respirator is cleaned and disinfected between users.

test.question: How must respirators be stored under 1910.134(h)(2)(i)?
options: Hung by the head straps on a nail or hook out in the work area so the facepiece can air dry between shifts, with the cartridges left attached so the change schedule tracking stays accurate and simple
Protected from damage, contamination, dust, sunlight, extreme temperatures, excessive moisture, and damaging chemicals, and stored to prevent deformation of the facepiece and exhalation valve
On the dashboard
With the tools
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. Respirators must be stored to protect them from damage, contamination, dust, sunlight, extreme temperatures, excessive moisture, and damaging chemicals, and packed to prevent deformation of the facepiece and exhalation valve (1910.134(h)(2)(i)). Job-site scenario: the half mask goes in a sealed bag in the gang box, not loose on the dashboard.

test.question: How often must the respiratory program be evaluated under 1910.134(l)(1)?
options: Only when an OSHA compliance officer requests it
Once when the written program is first adopted, with later reviews only when OSHA revises the respiratory protection standard
As necessary to ensure the written program is being effectively implemented and remains effective
Only after an employee fails a fit test or reports a respirator problem, and then only for that employee's work area
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. The employer must conduct workplace evaluations as necessary to ensure the written program is effectively implemented and continues to be effective (1910.134(l)(1)). Job-site scenario: the program administrator reviews the program when the job moves from demolition to coatings.

test.question: Under 1910.134(m)(2), how long must fit test records be kept?
options: For 30 years, the same as medical evaluation records
One year after the employee leaves the job
30 days after the test
Until the next fit test is administered
test.explanation: Under 1926.103, construction respiratory protection requirements are identical to 29 CFR 1910.134. The employer must keep a record of each employee's qualitative and quantitative fit tests (1910.134(m)(2)(i)), retained until the next fit test is administered (1910.134(m)(2)(ii)). A written copy of the current program must also be kept (1910.134(m)(3)). Job-site scenario: last year's fit test record stays on file until this year's test is done.

title: Noise Exposure and Hearing Conservation
topics: When ear protection must be provided
Measuring on the A-scale at slow response

resources.title: Hearing Conservation Program Requirement
resources.description: Continuing hearing conservation program and combined-exposure calculation

test.question: Under Table D-2 of 1926.52, what is the permissible noise exposure for 8 hours per day?
options: 85 dBA
90 dBA
95 dBA
100 dBA
test.explanation: Table D-2 permits 90 dBA (slow response) for 8 hours per day (1926.52(d)(1) Table D-2). Job-site scenario: a compactor operator at 92 dBA all shift exceeds the permissible exposure.

test.question: An employee works 4 hours at 95 dBA and 1 hour at 100 dBA. Using the formula in 1926.52(d)(2)(ii), does the exposure exceed the permissible level?
options: No; Fe = 0.5
Yes; Fe = 1.5
No; Fe = 1.0
It cannot be calculated
test.explanation: Fe = T1/L1 + T2/L2. With Table D-2 values L = 4 hours at 95 dBA and 2 hours at 100 dBA, Fe = 4/4 + 1/2 = 1.5. If Fe exceeds 1, the exposure exceeds permissible levels (1926.52(d)(2)(ii)). Job-site scenario: a saw operator's mixed day is over the limit even though neither period alone is.

test.question: Under 1926.101(a), when must ear protective devices be provided and used?
options: At any noise level above 85 dBA, before engineering or administrative controls are even considered
Only when exposure exceeds 105 dBA, after the employer has first tried engineering and administrative controls
Wherever it is not feasible to reduce noise levels or durations to those in Table D-2
Only when requested
test.explanation: Wherever it is not feasible to reduce noise levels or exposure durations to the Table D-2 values, ear protective devices must be provided and used (1926.101(a)). Inserts must be fitted individually by competent persons (1926.101(b)). Job-site scenario: after quieter equipment and rotation, the remaining exposure is handled with fitted earplugs.

test.question: What does 1926.52(d)(1) require when sound levels exceed the values in Table D-2?
options: Annual audiograms
Hearing protectors for each exposed worker, with no further program required
Monthly audiograms for each employee exposed above Table D-2
A continuing, effective hearing conservation program
test.explanation: In all cases where sound levels exceed Table D-2 values, a continuing, effective hearing conservation program must be administered (1926.52(d)(1)). 1926.52 does not spell out program elements such as annual audiograms; those are in the general-industry rule (1910.95). Job-site scenario: crews regularly over 90 dBA are enrolled in the company's hearing conservation program.

test.question: What does 1926.52(e) say about impulsive or impact noise?
options: It should not exceed 140 dB peak sound pressure level
It shall not exceed 115 dBA, the top continuous-noise level listed in Table D-2
It is not addressed
It should not exceed 120 dB peak sound pressure level for any single impulse
test.explanation: Exposure to impulsive or impact noise should not exceed 140 dB peak sound pressure level (1926.52(e)). Note that the text says "should" (recommended under 1926.32(r)), not "shall". Job-site scenario: powder-actuated tool use is planned to keep peak exposure below 140 dB.

test.question: Under 1926.52(c), how is noise with maxima at intervals of 1 second or less treated?
options: As impulse noise
As continuous noise
It is ignored
As intermittent noise
test.explanation: If variations in noise level involve maxima at intervals of 1 second or less, the noise is considered continuous (1926.52(c)). Job-site scenario: a jackhammer's rapid blows are treated as continuous noise for Table D-2.

test.question: Under 1926.52(b), what must be done first when sound levels exceed Table D-2?
options: Issue PPE only
Administrative controls only
Use feasible administrative or engineering controls; if they fail to bring levels within the table, provide and use PPE
Provide earmuffs rated NRR 25 or higher to each exposed worker
test.explanation: When sound levels exceed Table D-2, feasible administrative or engineering controls must be used. If they fail to bring levels within the table, PPE must be provided and used (1926.52(b)). Job-site scenario: an enclosure is put around the generator first; earplugs cover what remains.

test.question: Under Table D-2 of 1926.52, how long may an employee be exposed to 100 dBA per day?
options: 8 hours
4 hours
2 hours
1/2 hour
test.explanation: Table D-2 permits 2 hours per day at 100 dBA (1926.52(d)(1) Table D-2). Job-site scenario: a worker running a cut-off saw at 100 dBA without controls is limited to 2 hours.

test.question: How must sound levels be measured for comparison with Table D-2 under 1926.52(a)?
options: On the A-scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response
On the C-scale, fast response
With a smartphone app
By ear
test.explanation: Protection is required when sound levels exceed Table D-2 as measured on the A-scale of a standard sound level meter at slow response (1926.52(a)). Job-site scenario: the safety lead sets the meter to A-weighting, slow response, before surveying the saw cutting.

test.question: How long does Table D-2 of 1926.52 permit at 95 dBA?
options: 8 hours
6 hours
4 hours
2 hours
test.explanation: Table D-2 permits 4 hours per day at 95 dBA (1926.52(d)(1) Table D-2). Job-site scenario: a chipping-gun operator at 95 dBA is rotated off after 4 hours unless controls reduce the level.

resources.title: Working On or Near Exposed Energized Parts
resources.description: Qualified-employee, approach distance, arc hazard, and fuse handling rules

resources.title: PPE Requirements
resources.description: Personal protective equipment for line work

test.question: Under 1926.960(b)(1), who may work on exposed energized lines, or in areas with unguarded, uninsulated energized lines operating at 50 volts or more?
options: Any employee wearing rubber gloves
Any apprentice under supervision by radio
Only qualified employees
Anyone with a hard hat rated Class E
test.explanation: Only qualified employees may work on or with exposed energized lines or parts of equipment (1926.960(b)(1)(i)), or in areas containing unguarded, uninsulated energized lines or parts operating at 50 volts or more (1926.960(b)(1)(ii)). Lines are treated as energized unless deenergized under 1926.961 (1926.960(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: a laborer does not enter the open vault with energized cables; the qualified lineworker does.

test.question: Under 1926.960(h), what must an employee use to install or remove fuses with a terminal energized at more than 300 volts?
options: Bare hands with leather gloves
Any screwdriver
A wooden stick or broom handle
Tools or gloves rated for the voltage
test.explanation: When installing or removing fuses with one or both terminals energized at more than 300 volts, or with exposed parts energized at more than 50 volts, the employee must use tools or gloves rated for the voltage (1926.960(h)). Job-site scenario: a hot stick rated for the circuit is used to pull the cutout fuse.

test.question: When attaching a protective ground to a line, what order does 1926.962(f)(1) require?
options: Ground-end connection first, then the other end with a live-line tool
Line end first using a live-line tool, then the ground end, so the conductor is drained
Either end first, as long as both clamps are placed with a live-line tool
Both ends at once
test.explanation: The employee must attach the ground-end connection first, then attach the other end with a live-line tool. For 600 volts or less, other insulating equipment may be allowed (1926.962(f)(1)). Removal is the reverse: line end first with a live-line tool, then the ground end (1926.962(f)(2)). Job-site scenario: the crew clamps to the ground rod first, then uses a hot stick to put the clamp on the conductor.

test.question: Under 1926.960(g)(1), what must the employer assess for employees doing line work?
options: The line voltage only, to set minimum approach distances; arc hazards are covered by the utility's switching orders
The workplace, to identify employees exposed to hazards from flames or electric arcs
Only the weather
Each crew's first-aid and CPR training status
test.explanation: The employer must assess the workplace to identify employees exposed to hazards from flames or electric arcs (1926.960(g)(1)). For each exposed employee, it must make a reasonable estimate of incident heat energy (1926.960(g)(2)). Job-site scenario: the arc assessment for switching work drives the arc-rated clothing selection.

test.question: Per Table E-5 (1926.97(c)(2)(viii)), how often must rubber insulating gloves be electrically tested?
options: Monthly
Before first issue and every 12 months thereafter, when insulating value is suspect, after repair, and after any use without leather protectors
Before first issue and every 6 months thereafter, when insulating value is suspect, after repair, and after use without protectors
Only when visibly damaged
test.explanation: Electrical protective equipment must be periodically tested per Tables E-4 and E-5 (1926.97(c)(2)(viii)). Table E-5 sets rubber insulating gloves at before first issue and every 6 months thereafter, plus when insulating value is suspect, after repair, and after use without protectors. Sleeves and blankets are every 12 months. Job-site scenario: the glove tracking sheet shows test dates under 6 months old.

test.question: Under 1926.965(b), how must employees enter and exit a manhole or vault more than 4 feet deep?
options: By stepping on the cables
By jumping in
By climbing down the conduit duct bank
With a ladder or other climbing device, never by stepping on cables or hangers
test.explanation: Employees must use a ladder or other climbing device to enter and exit a manhole or subsurface vault more than 4 feet deep, and may not climb in or out by stepping on cables or hangers (1926.965(b)). While work is done in a manhole with energized equipment, an employee with first-aid training must be available at the surface (1926.965(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: a portable ladder is set in the vault before the splicer climbs down.

test.question: For field work by two or more employees on lines energized at 50 volts or more, how many first-aid trained persons does 1926.951(b)(1) require at the work location?
options: At least two
None
At least one
One per five employees
test.explanation: In addition to 1926.50, when employees work on or with exposed lines energized at 50 volts or more, field work involving two or more employees at a location needs at least two trained persons available (1926.951(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: a three-person line crew has two members with current first-aid/CPR cards.

test.question: Under 1926.952(c)(1), when work is repetitive and similar through the day, at least how many job briefings are required?
options: One at the end of each shift to review the day's work
At least one before the start of the first job of each day or shift
One at the start of each workweek, with additional briefings only when the crew changes
Only when a supervisor is present to lead it and record attendance on the tailboard form
test.explanation: If the work during the day or shift is repetitive and similar, at least one job briefing must be held before the start of the first job of each day or shift (1926.952(c)(1)). Additional briefings are required if significant changes occur (1926.952(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: the tailboard briefing happens before the first pole change of the day.

test.question: When working within reaching distance of exposed energized parts, what does 1926.960(f) require for items like rings and watches?
options: Remove rings only; watches with metal bands may stay on
Wear them under gloves
Remove them or render them nonconductive, unless they do not increase the hazard
Only remove keychains
test.explanation: The employer must ensure the employee removes or renders nonconductive all exposed conductive articles, such as keychains, watch chains, rings, or wristwatches and bands, unless they do not increase the hazard of contact (1926.960(f)). Job-site scenario: the lineworker takes off a wedding ring before working near the energized bus.

test.question: Under 1926.964(d)(4), what must happen during adverse weather when working on towers or structures (except emergency restoration)?
options: Continue working as long as employees stay tied off and tools are tethered, because following the required fall protection practices makes tower work safe in storms and high winds
Stop work only when the National Weather Service has issued a severe thunderstorm or winter storm warning for the county, and resume as soon as that warning expires or is cancelled
Continue with a ground observer posted to call the crew down once lightning is seen
Discontinue work when adverse weather (such as thunderstorms in the vicinity, high winds, snow or ice storms) would make the work hazardous despite the required practices
test.explanation: Except during emergency restoration, employees must discontinue work on towers and structures when adverse weather would make the work hazardous despite the required practices (1926.964(d)(4)). The note lists thunderstorms in the vicinity, high winds, snow storms, and ice storms as examples. Job-site scenario: the tower crew comes down when lightning is reported nearby.

title: Pile Driving and Site Clearing
topics: Overhead protection for pile driver operators
Rollover guards and canopies on clearing equipment

resources.title: Pile Driver General Requirements
resources.description: Overhead protection, blocking devices, and hose restraints

test.question: What overhead protection does 1926.603(a)(3) require for pile driving equipment?
options: Protection that does not obscure the operator's vision, equivalent to 2-inch planking or other solid material of equivalent strength
Overhead protection equal to 1-inch plywood sheathing
A canvas canopy
Only a hard hat
test.explanation: Overhead protection that will not obscure the operator's vision, and that meets Subpart N, must be provided. It must be the equivalent of 2-inch planking or other solid material of equivalent strength (1926.603(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: the pile driver cab roof is solid plate, not mesh.

test.question: Under 1926.603(a)(5), what must be placed in the leads while employees work under the hammer?
options: Nothing if the hammer is resting on the pile and the hoist brake is set and locked
A blocking device capable of safely supporting the weight of the hammer
A warning sign
A lockout tag on the hammer hoist controls, with the hammer lowered onto the pile head
test.explanation: A blocking device capable of safely supporting the hammer's weight must be placed in the leads under the hammer at all times while employees work under it (1926.603(a)(5)). Stop blocks must keep the hammer from being raised against the head block (1926.603(a)(4)). Job-site scenario: before changing the cushion, the crew pins the blocking device under the hammer.

test.question: How must the steam hose to a steam hammer be secured under 1926.603(a)(9)?
options: With duct tape
Securely attached to the pile driver leads with at least 1/8-inch diameter wire rope at 10-foot intervals along the hose, to keep it from whipping if the joint breaks
Securely attached to the hammer with an adequate length of at least 1/4-inch diameter chain or cable, to prevent whipping if the joint breaks
Tied to the leads with manila rope at the hose midpoint, so a broken hose swings freely away from the operator and clear of the hammer and the pile cap
test.explanation: Steam hose to a steam hammer or jet pipe must be secured to the hammer with an adequate length of at least 1/4-inch chain or cable to prevent whipping if the joint breaks. Air hammer hoses need the same protection (1926.603(a)(9)). Each hose connection needs safety chains or equivalent (1926.603(a)(10)). Job-site scenario: whip checks are on every air-hammer coupling.

test.question: Under 1926.603(a)(11), what must steam line controls consist of?
options: A single quick-acting lever valve at the boiler, with a pressure gauge mounted where the hammer operator can read it
A pressure gauge and a single gate valve at the boiler, with a relief valve set at the hammer's rated working pressure
No valves
Two shutoff valves, one of which is a quick-acting lever type within easy reach of the hammer operator
test.explanation: Steam line controls must consist of two shutoff valves, one a quick-acting lever type within easy reach of the hammer operator (1926.603(a)(11)). Job-site scenario: the operator can kill steam to the hammer with one lever pull.

test.question: Under 1926.603(c)(1), whom may pile driver engineers and winchmen accept signals from?
options: Only the designated signalmen
Anyone on the crew
The superintendent only
Any person who sees a problem, for all signals
test.explanation: Engineers and winchmen may accept signals only from the designated signalmen (1926.603(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: the winchman ignores waves from a passing laborer and watches the designated signalman.

test.question: What does 1926.603(c)(2) require while piling is being hoisted into the leads?
options: Workers steady the pile by hand underneath
All employees must be kept clear
Only the foreman may stay close
Hard hats for the crew only
test.explanation: All employees must be kept clear when piling is being hoisted into the leads (1926.603(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: the crew stands back until the pile is stabbed and set in the leads.

test.question: Piles are being driven in an excavated pit. What does 1926.603(c)(3) require for the pit walls?
options: Shore them with timber only if over 20 feet deep
Slope them at 1/2 horizontal to 1 vertical in any soil type, or bench them in 5-foot steps
Slope them to the angle of repose, or sheet-pile and brace them
Keep them vertical
test.explanation: When piles are driven in an excavated pit, the walls must be sloped to the angle of repose or sheet-piled and braced (1926.603(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: the pile cap pit is sheet-piled and braced before the driver works in it.

test.question: When the tops of driven piles must be cut off, what does 1926.603(c)(5) require?
options: Continue driving, provided the cutting crew stays at least one full length of the longest pile away from the driver's leads
Keep driving, provided a spotter watches the hammer and the cutting crew wears hard hats and stays outside the swing radius of the leads
Suspend pile driving only while the cutting crew is within 25 feet of the driver, and otherwise let both operations continue
Suspend pile driving, unless the cutting is at least twice the length of the longest pile away from the driver
test.explanation: Pile driving must be suspended when cutting off pile tops, except where the cutting is at least twice the length of the longest pile from the driver (1926.603(c)(5)). Job-site scenario: with 60-foot piles, cutoff crews work at least 120 feet from the active driver, or driving stops.

test.question: Under 1926.604(a)(1), how must employees doing site clearing be protected?
options: From the hazards of irritant and toxic plants, and suitably instructed in the first aid treatment available
Long sleeves only; first aid instruction is for the foreman
Only with gloves
Only with a hard hat
test.explanation: Employees engaged in site clearing must be protected from the hazards of irritant and toxic plants and be suitably instructed in the first aid treatment available (1926.604(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: the clearing crew gets long sleeves, barrier cream, and a briefing on poison oak exposure.

test.question: What protection does 1926.604(a)(2) require on rider-operated site clearing equipment?
options: A roll bar only, with no overhead or rear canopy guard
Rollover guards, plus an overhead and rear canopy guard (overhead of at least 1/8-inch steel plate or 1/4-inch woven wire mesh with openings no greater than 1 inch, or equivalent)
A seat belt only
A sunshade
test.explanation: All site clearing equipment must have rollover guards. Rider-operated equipment also needs an overhead and rear canopy guard: the overhead must be at least 1/8-inch steel plate or 1/4-inch woven wire mesh with openings no greater than 1 inch (or equivalent), and the rear opening covered with at least 1/4-inch woven wire mesh with openings no greater than 1 inch (1926.604(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: the dozer clearing timber has a screened canopy against falling limbs.

title: Underground Construction
topics: Mechanical ventilation and fresh air volume
Continuous gas monitoring at the face

resources.title: Air Quality and Monitoring
resources.description: Air monitoring requirements for underground construction

resources.title: Emergency Provisions
resources.description: Hoisting capability, self-rescuers, and rescue teams

test.question: Under 1926.800(j)(1)(ii)(A), what oxygen range must underground work area atmospheres be tested to assure?
options: At least 16.5%
At least 21%
At least 19.5% and no more than 22%
test.explanation: The atmosphere in all underground work areas must be tested as often as necessary to assure it contains at least 19.5% and no more than 22% oxygen (1926.800(j)(1)(ii)(A)). A competent person must perform the air monitoring (1926.800(j)(1)(i)(A)). Job-site scenario: the competent person checks oxygen at the heading before the shift goes in.

test.question: When is mechanical ventilation required in underground work areas under 1926.800(k)(1)(ii)?
options: Only when diesel equipment is operating underground
Only during welding
Only where the heading is more than 100 feet from the portal, or where air testing shows oxygen below 19.5 percent at the face
In all underground work areas, unless the employer can show natural ventilation provides the necessary air quality
test.explanation: Mechanical ventilation must be provided in all underground work areas unless the employer can demonstrate that natural ventilation provides the necessary air quality through sufficient volume and flow (1926.800(k)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: the tunnel runs a vent fan and duct to the face.

test.question: What does 1926.800(c) require for tracking people underground?
options: A check-in/check-out procedure so above-ground personnel can determine an accurate count of persons underground in an emergency
A sign-in log at the portal only, with no check-out required
Only new workers sign in
Optional sign-in
test.explanation: The employer must maintain a check-in/check-out procedure so above-ground personnel can determine an accurate count of persons underground in an emergency (1926.800(c)). The procedure is not required once underground facilities designed for human occupancy are sufficiently complete that permanent environmental controls are effective and the remaining work will not cause an environmental hazard or structural failure. Job-site scenario: brass tags on a board at the shaft collar show who is below.

test.question: What emergency equipment does 1926.800(g)(2) require to be immediately available to employees underground?
options: Only a first aid kit
NIOSH-approved self-rescuers at work stations where employees might be trapped by smoke or gas
A portable fire extinguisher at each heading and a stretcher at the shaft bottom, checked by the shift boss each day
Escape ladders at the shaft and an air horn at each heading
test.explanation: The employer must provide NIOSH-approved self-rescuers, immediately available to all employees at underground work stations where they might be trapped by smoke or gas (1926.800(g)(2)). Job-site scenario: each miner carries or has within reach a self-rescuer at the heading.

test.question: Under 1926.800(q)(1), when must drilling equipment be inspected?
options: Weekly by the equipment operator, with defects logged and corrected at the next scheduled maintenance
Monthly by the shift boss using the manufacturer's checklist, with defects tagged for the mechanic
By a competent person prior to each use, with safety defects corrected before use
Annually by a certified mechanic during the scheduled overhaul, with the record kept on the machine
test.explanation: A competent person must inspect all drilling and associated equipment before each use, and equipment defects affecting safety must be corrected before use (1926.800(q)(1)). Haulage equipment must be inspected by a competent person before each shift (1926.800(r)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: the jumbo is inspected before drilling the round.

test.question: Where are the illumination requirements for underground construction found, per 1926.800(l)(1)?
options: There are none
Any level the foreman likes
Daylight only
Table D-3 of 1926.56 (5 foot-candles for tunnels and shafts generally, 10 at the heading during drilling, mucking, and scaling)
test.explanation: Illumination requirements for underground construction are in Table D-3 of 1926.56 (1926.800(l)(1)). Table D-3 lists 5 foot-candles for tunnels, shafts, and general underground work areas, with at least 10 foot-candles at the tunnel and shaft heading during drilling, mucking, and scaling. Job-site scenario: extra lights are placed at the face during drilling.

test.question: When rapid excavation machines are used, what monitoring does 1926.800(j)(1)(iv) require?
options: A continuous flammable gas monitor operated at the face, with sensors as high and close to the cutter head as practicable
A methane test only when the machine is first started up
A weekly flammable gas test at the face by a competent person, with sensors mounted at floor level behind the cutter head where gas collects
A monthly test
test.explanation: When rapid excavation machines are used, a continuous flammable gas monitor must be operated at the face, with sensors placed as high and close to the front of the cutter head as practicable (1926.800(j)(1)(iv)). Job-site scenario: the TBM's methane monitor runs continuously at the cutter head.

test.question: Under 1926.800(f)(1), what communication is required when natural voice communication is ineffective?
options: Two-way radios at the surface only, with a bell signal code used between the bottom of the shaft and the work face
A power-assisted means of voice communication between the work face, the bottom of the shaft, and the surface
A telephone at the surface only, with hand signals relayed between the work face and the bottom of the shaft by a signalman
Air horn signals between the face and shaft bottom
test.explanation: When natural unassisted voice communication is ineffective, a power-assisted means of voice communication must be used between the work face, the bottom of the shaft, and the surface (1926.800(f)(1)). Job-site scenario: a hardwired phone system connects the heading, shaft bottom, and collar.

test.question: How much fresh air must be supplied for each employee underground under 1926.800(k)(2)?
options: 50 cubic feet per minute
100 cubic feet per minute per employee at the face
At least 200 cubic feet per minute
500 cubic feet per minute for the whole crew
test.explanation: At least 200 cubic feet of fresh air per minute must be supplied for each employee underground (1926.800(k)(2)). Job-site scenario: with 15 workers underground, the ventilation plan delivers at least 3,000 cfm of fresh air.

test.question: Under 1926.800(o)(1), how must portal openings and access areas be protected?
options: Left unguarded if the portal is cut into competent rock, provided the face above it is checked for loose rock and material by the shift boss at the start of each shift
Marked with warning signs and lighting at the portal, with loose rock on the adjacent slopes scaled at the start of the job and then inspected by the shift boss each week
Only lighting
Guarded by shoring, fencing, head walls, shotcreting, or equivalent, with adjacent areas scaled or secured against loose soil, rock, or fractured materials
test.explanation: Portal openings and access areas must be guarded by shoring, fencing, head walls, shotcreting, or equivalent protection. Adjacent areas must be scaled or secured to prevent loose soil, rock, or fractured materials from endangering the portal and access area (1926.800(o)(1)). Job-site scenario: the tunnel portal has a steel canopy and scaled face.

title: Aerial Lifts
topics: No belting off to adjacent structures
Body belts vs. personal fall arrest

resources.title: Boom Platform Requirements
resources.description: Specific requirements for extensible and articulating boom platforms

resources.title: Fall Protection Systems Criteria
resources.description: Personal fall arrest and restraint criteria referenced by 1926.453

test.question: Under 1926.453(a)(2), when may an aerial lift be "field modified" for uses other than those intended by the manufacturer?
options: With written certification by the manufacturer or an equivalent entity (e.g., a nationally recognized testing lab) that it meets ANSI A92.2-1969 and 1926.453 and is at least as safe as before
Whenever the operator thinks it is safe
With the superintendent's verbal approval

When a qualified mechanic inspects the modified lift, load tests it at 150 percent of rated capacity, and records the results in the lift's maintenance log before it returns to service on the job site
test.explanation: Aerial lifts may be field modified only if the modification is certified in writing by the manufacturer or an equivalent entity, such as a nationally recognized testing laboratory, as conforming to ANSI A92.2-1969 and the section and at least as safe as before (1926.453(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: a pipe rack welded onto a basket needs written certification before use.

test.question: Under 1926.453(b)(2)(i), how often must lift controls on extensible and articulating boom platforms be tested?
options: At the start of each workweek
Each day prior to use
Monthly, by the rental company
Annually, by a qualified mechanic
test.explanation: Lift controls must be tested each day before use to determine that they are in safe working condition (1926.453(b)(2)(i)). Job-site scenario: the operator runs the platform and ground controls through their functions before the first lift of the day.

test.question: Under 1926.453(b)(2)(ii), who may operate an aerial lift?
options: The rental agent
Anyone with a driver's license
Only authorized persons
Only the owner
test.explanation: Only authorized persons may operate an aerial lift (1926.453(b)(2)(ii)). Job-site scenario: the foreman keeps a list of employees authorized to run the boom lift.

test.question: While working from an aerial lift, may an employee tie off to an adjacent pole, structure, or equipment under 1926.453(b)(2)(iii)?
options: Yes, it is preferred
Yes, if the lift is stationary
Only to steel beams
No; belting off to an adjacent pole, structure, or equipment is not permitted
test.explanation: Belting off to an adjacent pole, structure, or equipment while working from an aerial lift is not permitted (1926.453(b)(2)(iii)). The lanyard attaches to the boom or basket (1926.453(b)(2)(v)). Job-site scenario: the electrician clips to the basket anchor, not the building steel.

test.question: What does 1926.453(b)(2)(iv) require of employees in the basket?
options: They must stand firmly on the basket floor and may not sit or climb on the edge of the basket or use planks, ladders, or other devices for a work position
They may step up onto the basket rails for extra reach when the work is just out of range, provided the boom is fully extended and a second worker in the basket steadies them
They may stand on the mid-rail or use a short stepladder inside the basket when wearing a body harness with the lanyard attached to the boom or basket anchor point
They may sit on the edge if tied off
test.explanation: Employees must always stand firmly on the basket floor and may not sit or climb on the edge of the basket or use planks, ladders, or other devices for a work position (1926.453(b)(2)(iv)). Job-site scenario: if the work is out of reach, reposition the boom instead of climbing the rail.

test.question: 1926.453(b)(2)(v) says a body belt and lanyard attached to the boom or basket must be worn. What does the note to that paragraph say about body belts?
options: Body belts remain acceptable for fall arrest
Since January 1, 1998, body belts are not acceptable as part of a personal fall arrest system (1926.502(d)); body belts in tethering or restraint systems are acceptable under 1926.502(e)
Body belts are banned entirely
Body belts are required instead of harnesses
test.explanation: The paragraph requires a body belt with a lanyard attached to the boom or basket (1926.453(b)(2)(v)). The note explains that, as of January 1, 1998, body belts are not acceptable as part of a personal fall arrest system under 1926.502(d), but a body belt in a tethering or restraint system is acceptable under 1926.502(e). Job-site scenario: in a boom lift, a short restraint lanyard prevents ejection; for fall arrest, a full-body harness is used.

test.question: Under 1926.453(b)(2)(vi), what limits apply to the boom and basket?
options: Whatever the crew can lift into the basket
Two people maximum plus 50 pounds of tools, whatever the platform decal shows
Load limits specified by the manufacturer must not be exceeded
The supervisor's posted limit, which may exceed the decal rating if the basket is retested at 125 percent
test.explanation: Boom and basket load limits specified by the manufacturer must not be exceeded (1926.453(b)(2)(vi)). Job-site scenario: two workers plus a box of conduit are checked against the platform capacity decal.

test.question: What does 1926.453(b)(2)(vii) require when setting up an aerial lift?
options: Brakes released so the chassis settles level on the outriggers
Parking brake set and outriggers on pads, with wheel chocks used only when the lift will be left parked and unattended on the slope
Outriggers extended to full width on any ground surface, with the brakes set and wheel chocks needed only on grades steeper than 10 percent or on wet ground
Brakes set; outriggers, when used, positioned on pads or a solid surface; and wheel chocks installed on an incline when they can be safely installed
test.explanation: The brakes must be set, outriggers (when used) positioned on pads or a solid surface, and wheel chocks installed before using an aerial lift on an incline, provided they can be safely installed (1926.453(b)(2)(vii)). Job-site scenario: outrigger pads go under each foot on the soft lot.

test.question: Under 1926.453(b)(2)(viii), may an aerial lift truck be moved with the boom elevated and workers in the basket?
options: No, except equipment specifically designed for that type of operation
Yes, at walking speed
Yes, if a spotter walks alongside and the boom is raised no more than 10 feet above the cradle
Yes, on level ground
test.explanation: An aerial lift truck may not be moved when the boom is elevated in a working position with workers in the basket, except equipment specifically designed for this operation under (a)(1) and (2) (1926.453(b)(2)(viii)). Before moving the lift for travel, the boom must be inspected to confirm it is properly cradled and outriggers are stowed, except for equipment designed for travel with an elevated boom (1926.453(b)(2)(xii)). Job-site scenario: the truck-mounted bucket comes down before repositioning.

test.question: Under 1926.453(b)(2)(ix), when may the lower (ground) controls of a boom platform be operated?
options: Only after the shift supervisor approves by radio
Only with permission from the employee in the lift, except in an emergency
By any trained ground worker who needs to reposition the basket, without contacting the employee in the lift
Only in an emergency
test.explanation: Boom platforms designed as personnel carriers must have both upper and lower controls, and lower controls must be able to override the upper ones. Lower controls may not be operated unless permission has been obtained from the employee in the lift, except in an emergency (1926.453(b)(2)(ix)). Job-site scenario: the ground worker asks over the radio before touching the base controls.

title: Gases, Vapors, Fumes, Dusts, Mists, and Ventilation

resources.title: Gases, Vapors, Fumes, Dusts, and Mists
eCFR: 29 CFR 1926.55
resources.description: Current text, including Table 1 exposure limits

test.question: Under 1926.55(a)(2), how is exposure to a substance in Table 1 without a "(C)" designation measured against its limit?
options: As an instantaneous peak
As a weekly average
As an 8-hour time-weighted average in any work shift, from breathing-zone samples
As an annual average
test.explanation: For substances whose limit is not preceded by (C), exposure determined from breathing-zone air samples may not exceed the limit as an 8-hour time-weighted average in any work shift (1926.55(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: a painter's solvent exposure is sampled over the shift and compared to the TWA.

test.question: Under 1926.55(a)(1), what does a "(C)" before a limit in Table 1 mean?
options: A cancer warning
A 10-hour TWA that may be exceeded briefly, provided excursions stay under three times the limit for no more than 30 minutes
A recommended value only
A ceiling value that may never be exceeded (assessed as a 15-minute TWA if instantaneous monitoring is not feasible)
test.explanation: Substances with limits preceded by (C) are ceiling values: exposure may at no time exceed the limit. If instantaneous monitoring is not feasible, the ceiling is assessed as a 15-minute TWA that may not be exceeded at any time during the day (1926.55(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: short bursts of a ceiling-limited vapor during mixing are checked with a 15-minute sample.

test.question: Under 1926.55(b), what must be implemented first to meet the exposure limits?
options: Administrative or engineering controls, whenever feasible; protective equipment is used when they cannot achieve full compliance
Respirators issued to each exposed employee, with ventilation and work-practice controls added later only if fit testing shows the respirators cannot meet the limit
Shorter breaks
Quarterly personal air sampling for each exposed employee, with controls required only after two consecutive samples exceed the Table 1 limit
test.explanation: Administrative or engineering controls must first be implemented whenever feasible. When they cannot achieve full compliance, protective equipment or other protective measures must keep exposures within limits (1926.55(b)). Job-site scenario: a ventilation fan is set up in the garage before respirators are considered.

test.question: What is the permissible exposure limit for carbon monoxide in Table 1 of 1926.55?
options: 25 ppm
35 ppm
50 ppm
200 ppm
test.explanation: Table 1 to 1926.55 lists carbon monoxide at 50 ppm (55 mg/m3) as an 8-hour TWA (1926.55(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: propane heaters in an enclosed level are monitored to keep CO below 50 ppm TWA. Temporary heaters also need adequate fresh air (1926.154(a)(1)).

test.question: Under 1926.55(c), does the 1926.55 exposure table apply to asbestos?
options: Yes; Table 1 sets the asbestos limit at 2 fibers per cubic centimeter
Only indoors
No; asbestos exposure is governed by 1926.1101
Only for renovation work; demolition uses Table 1
test.explanation: Paragraphs (a) and (b) of 1926.55 do not apply to airborne asbestos, tremolite, anthophyllite, or actinolite. 1926.1101 applies instead (1926.55(c)). Formaldehyde is likewise excluded and governed by 1910.1048 (1926.55(d)). Job-site scenario: asbestos abatement follows 1926.1101 (Week 38), not Table 1.

test.question: Under 1926.57(a), when ventilation is used as an engineering control, how must the system be installed and operated?
options: Per the fan supplier's setup sheet, with no further checks
According to the general industry ventilation rules in 1910.94
Per local building code
According to the requirements of 1926.57
test.explanation: Concentrations of hazardous dusts, fumes, mists, vapors, or gases may not exceed the 1926.55(a) limits. When ventilation is used as an engineering control, the system must be installed and operated according to 1926.57 (1926.57(a)). Job-site scenario: the exhaust setup for a solvent-cleaning task is checked against 1926.57.

test.question: Under 1926.57(b), how must local exhaust ventilation be designed?
options: To prevent dispersion of contaminants in harmful concentrations, without drawing them through employees' work area
To blow contaminants toward the workers
Only to cool the area
Any design
test.explanation: Local exhaust must be designed to prevent dispersion of dusts, fumes, mists, vapors, and gases in harmful concentrations, and must not draw them through the employees' work area (1926.57(b)). Job-site scenario: the fume extractor hood is placed so the plume moves away from the welder's face, not across it.

test.question: Under 1926.57(d)(1), how long must an exhaust system run?
options: Only while the operation is under way, shutting off as soon as cutting stops so cleanup dust is not drawn into the duct
Continually during the operations it serves, and after they stop if employees remain in the contaminated zone
Only when someone complains
Only at shift end
test.explanation: The exhaust system must operate continually during all operations it is designed to serve. If an employee remains in the contaminated zone, it must keep running after the operation stops (1926.57(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: the dust collector keeps running after cutting stops while the crew cleans up.

test.question: Under 1926.57(e), where must collected contaminants from an exhaust system be discharged?
options: Back into the work area always
Into the stairwell
To the outside atmosphere (recirculation is allowed only if it does not cause harmful exposure)
Anywhere
test.explanation: The air outlet of every dust separator, and the contaminants collected by an exhaust system, must discharge to the outside atmosphere. Systems returning air to the work area may be used only if accumulated concentrations do not cause harmful exposure (1926.57(e)). Job-site scenario: the negative-air duct is run out a window, not into the hallway.

test.question: What respirators does 1926.57(f)(5)(i) require for protection from abrasive-blasting dusts?
options: Any respirator labeled to ANSI Z88.2 or the European EN 149 standard
Bandanas
Non-approved nuisance dust masks worn under a face shield
Only respirators approved by NIOSH under 42 CFR part 84
test.explanation: Employers must use only NIOSH-approved respirators (42 CFR part 84) to protect employees from dusts produced during abrasive blasting (1926.57(f)(5)(i)). Abrasive-blasting respirators must be worn by operators in specified situations (1926.57(f)(5)(ii)). Job-site scenario: the sandblaster wears a NIOSH-approved supplied-air blast hood.

title: Silica Exposure Control
topics: Written exposure control plan and restricting access

resources.title: eCFR: 29 CFR 1926.1153
resources.description: Current official text of the construction silica standard

test.question: Under 1926.1153(d)(1), what is the permissible exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica?
options: 25 µg/m3
50 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA
150 µg/m3 as a 15-minute short-term limit
test.explanation: No employee may be exposed to respirable crystalline silica above 50 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA (1926.1153(d)(1)). The action level is 25 µg/m3 (1926.1153(b) (definitions)). Job-site scenario: concrete grinding exposure is kept at or below 50 µg/m3.

test.question: When the employer is not fully following Table 1, whose exposure must it assess under 1926.1153(d)(2)(i)?
options: No one until the project ends, when a single area sample from the middle of the site is applied to the whole crew
Each employee who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level (25 µg/m3)
Only employees exposed above the PEL of 50 µg/m3, assessed by a single sample taken on the first day of the task
Only supervisors and competent persons, since the crew is covered by the supervisor's personal breathing zone sample
test.explanation: For tasks not on Table 1, or where Table 1 is not fully implemented, the employer must assess the exposure of each employee who is or may reasonably be expected to be exposed at or above the action level, using the performance or scheduled monitoring option (1926.1153(d)(2)(i)). Job-site scenario: a crew cutting brick with a method not on Table 1 gets air sampling.

test.question: Under 1926.1153(d)(3)(i), what must be used first to reduce silica exposure to the PEL?
options: Respirators
Time limits only
Engineering and work practice controls, unless not feasible
Training only
test.explanation: The employer must use engineering and work practice controls to reduce exposure to or below the PEL unless it can show they are not feasible. Where they are not sufficient, they must still be used to reduce exposure as low as feasible, supplemented by respirators (1926.1153(d)(3)(i)). Job-site scenario: a wet saw or vacuum shroud comes before relying on respirators.

test.question: Under 1926.1153(h)(1)(i), which employees must be offered medical surveillance?
options: Every employee on a site where silica work occurs, offered once at hire and then every five years for as long as they remain employed
Each employee exposed above the PEL for 30 or more days per year, whether or not a respirator is required, provided at no cost
Only supervisors
Each employee who will be required to use a respirator under the standard for 30 or more days per year, at no cost
test.explanation: Medical surveillance must be made available at no cost, at a reasonable time and place, to each employee who will be required to use a respirator under the standard for 30 or more days per year (1926.1153(h)(1)(i)). Periodic exams are at least every three years (1926.1153(h)(3)). Job-site scenario: a chipper who will wear a respirator more than 30 days this year is offered the exam.

test.question: What does 1926.1153(f)(1) say about dry sweeping silica dust?
options: It is not allowed where it could contribute to exposure, unless wet sweeping, HEPA vacuuming, or other low-dust methods are not feasible
It is always allowed
It is allowed with a fan
It is allowed outdoors only
test.explanation: Dry sweeping or dry brushing is not allowed where it could contribute to exposure unless wet sweeping, HEPA vacuuming, or other methods that minimize airborne dust are not feasible (1926.1153(f)(1)). Compressed air for cleaning is restricted too (1926.1153(f)(2)). Job-site scenario: the crew HEPA-vacuums slurry dust instead of sweeping it.

test.question: The construction silica standard has no "regulated area" requirement. What does 1926.1153(g)(1)(iv) require instead?
options: Warning tape around each cutting task, with no written procedures
The written exposure control plan must describe procedures to restrict access to work areas when necessary, to minimize the number of employees exposed and their exposure
Signs only
A regulated area marked with DANGER signs at each entrance, with access limited to authorized persons wearing respirators, as set out in the general industry silica standard, 1910.1053
test.explanation: The written exposure control plan must describe the procedures used to restrict access to work areas when necessary, to minimize the number of employees exposed and their exposure, including exposures from other employers (1926.1153(g)(1)(iv)). Regulated areas appear in the general-industry silica standard (1910.1053), not 1926.1153. Job-site scenario: the plan says other trades stay out of the cut-off saw zone.

test.question: Per Table 1 of 1926.1153(c)(1), what respiratory protection is required for an outdoor jackhammer with a continuous water spray at the point of impact?
options: APF 10 at all times
APF 25 at all times
None for 4 hours or less per shift; APF 10 for more than 4 hours
None for 8 hours or less; APF 10 beyond 8 hours
test.explanation: For jackhammers and handheld chipping tools used outdoors with water delivery at the point of impact, Table 1 lists no respirator for 4 hours or less per shift and APF 10 for more than 4 hours (1926.1153(c)(1) Table 1). Indoors or in enclosed areas, it is APF 10 for both. Job-site scenario: a 6-hour outdoor demo shift with water calls for an APF 10 respirator.

test.question: What does 1926.1153(i)(2)(i) require of silica training?
options: Each covered employee must watch a one-time silica awareness video and sign an attendance roster, while demonstrated knowledge of the hazards, tasks, and controls is required only of the competent person and supervisors
Monthly classes
Only hazard communication training on silica SDSs and labels
Each covered employee must be able to demonstrate knowledge of the health hazards, the specific exposure tasks, the protective measures in place, and the contents of the section, among other items
test.explanation: The employer must ensure each covered employee can demonstrate knowledge and understanding of at least: the health hazards, the specific tasks that could cause exposure, the protective measures implemented, the contents of the section, and the other listed items (1926.1153(i)(2)(i)). Job-site scenario: a new mason can explain which tasks create silica dust and which controls apply.

test.question: How must silica exposure and medical surveillance records be maintained under 1926.1153(j)?
options: Maintained and made available in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.1020
Kept for the duration of employment plus one year, as required by 29 CFR 1904
Given to each employee to keep, with no copy retained by the employer
Kept by the employer for 5 years
test.explanation: Exposure records (1926.1153(j)(1)(iii)), objective data (1926.1153(j)(2)(iii)), and medical records (1926.1153(j)(3)(iii)) must be maintained and made available in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.1020. Job-site scenario: air sampling results go into the company's 1910.1020 records system.

test.question: Under 1926.1153(g)(4), what must the competent person do?
options: Inspect each job site once before the work begins and certify in writing to the employer that the exposure control plan has been put into place
Make frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials, and equipment to implement the written exposure control plan
Order respirators and fit test every worker before the first silica task, leaving job site and equipment inspections to the crew foreman
Check equipment only when a worker reports a problem
test.explanation: The employer must designate a competent person to make frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials, and equipment to implement the written exposure control plan (1926.1153(g)(4)). The plan must be reviewed at least annually (1926.1153(g)(2)). Job-site scenario: the competent person checks that saws have working water feeds each day.

test.question: What is the action level for airborne lead in 1926.62(b)?
options: 30 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA, measured inside the employee's respirator facepiece
30 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA, without regard to respirators
50 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA, measured outside the respirator in the breathing zone
75 µg/m3
test.explanation: The action level is an airborne lead concentration of 30 µg/m3 averaged over an 8-hour period, without regard to respirator use (1926.62(b) (definitions)). Job-site scenario: a paint-removal crew sampled at 35 µg/m3 is above the action level.

test.question: Under 1926.62(j)(1)(ii), which employees must be covered by the full medical surveillance program under paragraphs (j)(2) and (j)(3)?
options: Employees who are or may be exposed at or above the action level for more than 90 days in any consecutive 12 months on the same project
Employees who are or may be exposed above the PEL for more than 30 days in any consecutive 12 months, as measured inside their respirators
Employees whose blood lead level is at or above 50 µg/dl on two tests
Employees who are or may be exposed at or above the action level for more than 30 days in any consecutive 12 months
test.explanation: A medical surveillance program under (j)(2) and (j)(3) is required for employees who are or may be exposed at or above the action level for more than 30 days in any consecutive 12 months (1926.62(j)(1)(ii)). Initial medical surveillance applies on any day at or above the action level (1926.62(j)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: a bridge-painting crew exposed above 30 µg/m3 for 40 days this year gets blood lead testing.

test.question: Under 1926.62(f)(1), when must respirators be used?
options: During periods when exposure exceeds the PEL, when engineering and work practice controls are insufficient, when an employee requests a respirator, and in the other listed situations
Only when a supervisor approves
Only at the action level
Only when exposure exceeds the PEL, with no respirator provided on an employee's request
test.explanation: Respirators must be used during periods when exposure exceeds the PEL (1926.62(f)(1)(i)), during operations where engineering and work practice controls are not sufficient (1926.62(f)(1)(ii)), during periods when an employee requests a respirator (1926.62(f)(1)(iii)), and in the other listed cases. Job-site scenario: abrasive blasting of lead paint above the PEL requires respirators while controls are installed.

test.question: Under 1926.62(d)(6)(iii), how often must monitoring be repeated if exposure is above the PEL?
options: Annually
Quarterly, until two consecutive measurements at least 7 days apart are at or below the PEL (then every 6 months if at or above the action level)
Monthly
Every 6 months, until two consecutive measurements at least 7 days apart are below the action level
test.explanation: If exposure is above the PEL, monitoring must be quarterly until at least two consecutive measurements, at least 7 days apart, are at or below the PEL (1926.62(d)(6)(iii)). Between the action level and the PEL, monitoring is at least every 6 months (1926.62(d)(6)(ii)). Job-site scenario: a crew at 70 µg/m3 is resampled every quarter.

test.question: What hygiene facilities does 1926.62(i) require for employees exposed above the PEL?
options: Change areas only; showers and eating areas are at the employer's option
Only a hand-wash station
Clean change areas, shower facilities where feasible, and lunchroom or eating areas
Only a trash can
test.explanation: For employees whose airborne exposure is above the PEL, the employer must provide clean change areas (1926.62(i)(2)(i)), showers where feasible (1926.62(i)(3)(i)), and lunchroom or eating facilities (1926.62(i)(4)(i)). Where showers are not provided, employees must wash hands and face at the end of the shift. Job-site scenario: a decon trailer with a change room and shower is set up for the abatement crew.

test.question: Under 1926.62(k)(1)(i), when must an employee be temporarily removed from lead exposure at or above the action level?
options: When the employee requests it after a blood level above 40 µg/dl
