When a single periodic blood test shows a blood lead level at or above 40 µg/dl, without waiting for a follow-up test
At age 50
When a periodic and a follow-up blood test both show a blood lead level at or above 50 µg/dl
test.explanation: The employer must remove an employee from work with exposure at or above the action level each time a periodic and a follow-up blood test both show a blood lead level at or above 50 µg/dl (1926.62(k)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: a painter with two results above 50 µg/dl is reassigned away from lead exposure, with removal protection.

test.question: How must floors and surfaces with lead accumulations be cleaned under 1926.62(h)?
options: By HEPA vacuuming or other low-dust methods where possible; sweeping only if vacuuming was tried and found ineffective; no compressed air unless used with a capturing ventilation system
By dry sweeping and shoveling first, using a vacuum only if sweeping leaves visible dust; any shop vacuum will do, and compressed air may blow dust off ledges and beams if workers wear respirators
With a leaf blower
Wet sweeping first, since wetting the dust keeps lead from becoming airborne
test.explanation: Clean-up must use vacuuming or other methods that minimize airborne lead wherever possible (1926.62(h)(2)). Shoveling and dry or wet sweeping are allowed only where vacuuming has been tried and found ineffective (1926.62(h)(3)). Vacuums must have HEPA filters (1926.62(h)(4)), and compressed air may not be used unless paired with capturing ventilation (1926.62(h)(5)). Job-site scenario: paint chips are HEPA-vacuumed off the deck.

test.question: Under 1926.62(l)(1), when must lead training be given?
options: Within the first week on the job, then a refresher only when an employee's blood lead test comes back at or above 40 µg/dl
Before job assignment, and at least annually for each employee exposed at or above the action level on any day
Within 30 days after job assignment, and then every three years for employees exposed above the PEL for more than 30 days a year
At initial hire only, for employees exposed above the PEL
test.explanation: Training must be given before job assignment (1926.62(l)(1)(iii)) and at least annually for each employee exposed at or above the action level on any day (1926.62(l)(1)(iv)). Job-site scenario: returning abatement workers get annual lead training.

test.question: What do the required warning signs say under 1926.62(m)(1)(i), and where are they posted?
options: "CAUTION/LEAD HAZARD/MAY DAMAGE FERTILITY OR THE UNBORN CHILD/CAUSES DAMAGE TO THE CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM/WASH HANDS BEFORE EATING", at the site entrance gate once exposure reaches the action level
"WARNING/LEAD WORK AREA/POISON/NO SMOKING OR EATING", in each work area above the PEL
"DANGER/LEAD WORK AREA/MAY DAMAGE FERTILITY OR THE UNBORN CHILD/CAUSES DAMAGE TO THE CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM/DO NOT EAT, DRINK OR SMOKE IN THIS AREA", in each work area above the PEL
"Keep Out" at the gate only
test.explanation: Warning signs with that legend must be posted in each work area where exposure is above the PEL (1926.62(m)(1)(i)). Before June 1, 2016, the older "WARNING / LEAD WORK AREA / POISON / NO SMOKING OR EATING" legend was allowed (1926.62(m)(1)(v)). Job-site scenario: the containment entrance on the bridge has the DANGER lead sign.

test.question: Under 1926.62(c)(1), what is the permissible exposure limit for lead?
options: 30 µg/m3 averaged over an 8-hour shift
50 µg/m3 as an 8-hour TWA
100 µg/m3 as a 15-minute short-term limit
test.explanation: No employee may be exposed to lead above 50 µg/m3 averaged over an 8-hour period (1926.62(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: monitoring shows 45 µg/m3, which is above the action level but within the PEL.

title: Asbestos Awareness
topics: Identifying ACM and PACM before work

test.question: Under 1926.1101(k)(3)(i), what must employers do before work begins in areas containing ACM or PACM?
options: Identify the presence, location, and quantity of ACM and/or PACM
Presume materials are asbestos-free unless the owner already has a survey showing ACM in the area
Sample the air for asbestos fibers once work has started, and stop work if levels exceed the PEL
Rely on the owner to flag any ACM it happens to know about
test.explanation: Before work in areas containing ACM and PACM begins, employers must identify the presence, location, and quantity of ACM and/or PACM (1926.1101(k)(3)(i)). Thermal system insulation and surfacing material in buildings constructed no later than 1980 is presumed asbestos-containing (PACM) unless rebutted (1926.1101(b) (definitions)). Job-site scenario: before demolishing a 1970s ceiling, the GC confirms whether the spray-on fireproofing has been tested.

test.question: What are the asbestos exposure limits in 1926.1101(c)?
options: 1 f/cc TWA only
0.1 f/cc as an 8-hour TWA, and 1.0 f/cc averaged over 30 minutes (excursion limit)
5 f/cc
0.1 f/cc as an 8-hour TWA, with no short-term limit
test.explanation: No employee may be exposed above 0.1 fiber per cubic centimeter as an 8-hour TWA (1926.1101(c)(1)), or above 1.0 f/cc averaged over a 30-minute sampling period (1926.1101(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: monitoring during pipe insulation removal is compared to both limits.

test.question: Under 1926.1101(b), what is Class I asbestos work?
options: Removal of ACM floor tile, wallboard, roofing shingles, and construction mastics
Repair and maintenance work where TSI or surfacing ACM is likely to be disturbed
Removal of thermal system insulation (TSI) and surfacing ACM and PACM
Custodial cleanup
test.explanation: Class I asbestos work means removal of TSI and surfacing ACM and PACM (1926.1101(b) (definitions)). Class II is removal of other ACM, such as wallboard, floor tile, and roofing. Job-site scenario: stripping pipe lagging in a boiler room is Class I.

test.question: What does 1926.1101(g)(1)(ii) require to control exposure during asbestos handling and removal?
options: Dry removal with HEPA-filtered vacuums, followed by dry sweeping of remaining debris
Compressed air to blow debris off surfaces, with a respirator on each worker
No controls
Wet methods or wetting agents, except where shown infeasible
test.explanation: Wet methods or wetting agents must be used to control exposure during handling, mixing, removal, cutting, application, and cleanup, unless the employer shows wet methods are infeasible (1926.1101(g)(1)(ii)). Amended water is water with a surfactant added to penetrate ACM (1926.1101(b) (definitions)). Job-site scenario: floor tile is misted with amended water before removal.

test.question: Under 1926.1101(h)(1), which work always requires respirators?
options: Class I asbestos work (among other listed situations, such as Class II work when ACM is not removed substantially intact)
All Class II work, including floor tile and roofing shingles removed substantially intact with wet methods after a negative exposure assessment
Class IV custodial cleanup outside regulated areas where no one else is required to wear respirators
Any Class III repair work, even with wet methods and a negative exposure assessment
test.explanation: Respirators are required during all Class I work (1926.1101(h)(1)(i)), during Class II work when ACM is not removed in a substantially intact state (1926.1101(h)(1)(ii)), and in other listed situations. Job-site scenario: the TSI removal crew wears respirators regardless of monitoring results.

test.question: How must asbestos-contaminated waste and debris be disposed of under 1926.1101(g)(1)(iii)?
options: Promptly, in the regular site trash or an open dumpster after being wetted down with amended water
Promptly, in leak-tight containers (except in roofing operations covered elsewhere)
Collected at the end of the project and placed in covered roll-off dumpsters lined with plastic
Burned on site
test.explanation: Wastes and debris contaminated with asbestos must be promptly cleaned up and disposed of in leak-tight containers, except in roofing operations under (g)(8)(ii) (1926.1101(g)(1)(iii)). Job-site scenario: bagged debris is sealed and labeled before leaving the regulated area.

test.question: For Class I jobs involving over 25 linear or 10 square feet of TSI or surfacing ACM/PACM, what decontamination area does 1926.1101(j)(1)(i) require?
options: A single room
A hose outside
An equipment room, shower area, and clean room in series, adjacent and connected to the regulated area
A clean room and equipment room only, with workers showering at home
test.explanation: A decontamination area adjacent and connected to the regulated area is required, consisting of an equipment room, shower area, and clean room in series (1926.1101(j)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: the three-stage decon unit is built at the containment entrance.

test.question: Under 1926.1101(e)(6), who must supervise asbestos work in regulated areas?
options: A foreman with only OSHA 10 training
Each worker, using buddy checks
The project manager
A competent person as defined in 1926.1101(b)
test.explanation: All asbestos work in regulated areas must be supervised by a competent person as defined in paragraph (b) (1926.1101(e)(6)). All Class I, II, and III work must be done within regulated areas (1926.1101(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: the abatement contractor's trained competent person is on site during removal.

test.question: What must regulated-area warning signs say under 1926.1101(k)(7)(ii)(A)?
options: "DANGER / ASBESTOS / MAY CAUSE CANCER / CAUSES DAMAGE TO LUNGS / AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY"
"CAUTION / ASBESTOS DUST HAZARD / AVOID BREATHING DUST / MAY CAUSE CANCER / WEAR RESPIRATORS IN THIS AREA"
"Keep Out"
"DANGER / ASBESTOS / CANCER AND LUNG DISEASE HAZARD / AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY"
test.explanation: Warning signs demarcating the regulated area must bear: DANGER / ASBESTOS / MAY CAUSE CANCER / CAUSES DAMAGE TO LUNGS / AUTHORIZED PERSONNEL ONLY (1926.1101(k)(7)(ii)(A)). Where respirators and protective clothing are required, the signs must also say so (1926.1101(k)(7)(ii)(B)). Job-site scenario: signs are posted far enough out to read before entering.

test.question: How long must asbestos medical surveillance records be kept under 1926.1101(n)(3)(iii)?
options: 1 year
For the duration of employment plus 30 years, per 1910.1020
For 5 years after the employee leaves, the same period as OSHA 300 logs
For the duration of employment only
test.explanation: Medical surveillance records must be kept for the duration of employment plus 30 years, in accordance with 1910.1020 (1926.1101(n)(3)(iii)). Job-site scenario: the abatement firm keeps workers' medical records long after they leave.

resources.title: Evacuation Plans and Procedures eTool
resources.description: OSHA eTool for emergency action and evacuation planning

test.question: Which is one of the minimum elements of an emergency action plan under 1926.35(b)?
options: Exit routes only
Rescue and medical duties for every employee on site, whether or not they are assigned to perform them
The preferred means of reporting fires and other emergencies
Procedures for all employees to stay and shut down their equipment before they evacuate
test.explanation: Minimum elements include escape procedures and route assignments, procedures for employees who stay to run critical operations, procedures to account for all employees after evacuation, rescue and medical duties, the preferred means of reporting emergencies, and contacts for more information (1926.35(b)(1)-(6)). Job-site scenario: the plan says to report fires by air horn and radio call to the site office.

test.question: Under 1926.35(e)(2), when must the employer review the plan with each covered employee?
options: Only once at hire
Annually only
Monthly
When the plan is developed, whenever the employee's responsibilities or designated actions change, and whenever the plan changes
test.explanation: The employer must review the plan with each covered employee initially when the plan is developed, whenever the employee's responsibilities or actions under the plan change, and whenever the plan changes (1926.35(e)(2)). Job-site scenario: when a new fuel storage area changes the escape route, the crew is re-briefed.

test.question: Under 1926.35(e)(1), what must happen before the plan is implemented?
options: The employer must designate and train enough persons to assist in safe and orderly evacuation
The local fire department must designate and train evacuation assistants
Only post a map
Hire an outside consultant
test.explanation: Before implementing the plan, the employer must designate and train a sufficient number of persons to assist in the safe and orderly emergency evacuation of employees (1926.35(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: floor wardens are trained on each level of the high-rise job.

test.question: If the employee alarm system is used for more than one purpose, what does 1926.35(c)(2) require?
options: One common signal, followed by a voice announcement
A distinctive signal for each purpose
Voice announcements by radio instead of alarm signals
No alarm
test.explanation: If the alarm system is used to alert fire brigade members or for other purposes, a distinctive signal must be used for each purpose (1926.35(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: evacuation is a continuous horn; tornado shelter is three short blasts.

test.question: What must the emergency action plan establish under 1926.35(d)?
options: Only the outdoor assembly point, with evacuation types left to the fire department on arrival
A single full-site evacuation procedure used for every type of emergency
The types of evacuation to be used in emergency circumstances
Nothing about evacuation, since routes are covered in the fire prevention plan
test.explanation: The employer must establish in the plan the types of evacuation to be used in emergencies (1926.35(d)). Job-site scenario: the plan distinguishes full-site evacuation for fire from partial evacuation for a gas leak in one area.

test.question: Under 1926.35(b)(6), whom must the plan identify?
options: Only outside emergency responders, such as the local fire department and ambulance service, each listed by agency name and 24-hour dispatch phone number
Each employee's personal emergency contact or next of kin, listed by name and phone number, so families can be notified after an evacuation or injury on the site
The OSHA area office that would investigate an incident on the site
Names or regular job titles of persons or departments who can be contacted for more information or explanation of duties under the plan
test.explanation: The plan must include the names or regular job titles of persons or departments who can be contacted for more information or explanation of duties under the plan (1926.35(b)(6)). Job-site scenario: the plan lists the site safety manager's title and phone.

test.question: Under 1926.35(a), when must an emergency action plan be in writing?
options: When required by a particular OSHA standard; it must be written except that employers with 10 or fewer employees may communicate it orally
Only for jobs inside enclosed buildings, not open-air or road work
When required by a particular OSHA standard; it must be written except that employers with 25 or fewer employees on site may communicate it orally to the crew
Only on federal contracts or jobs with more than 50 employees; other employers may leave the plan unwritten and post evacuation route maps instead
test.explanation: Section 1926.35 applies to emergency action plans required by a particular OSHA standard. The plan must be in writing, except as provided in the last sentence of (e)(3) for employers with 10 or fewer employees (1926.35(a)). Job-site scenario: a 40-person job site under a standard requiring an EAP keeps a written plan in the trailer.

test.question: What does 1926.35(b)(3) require the plan to include?
options: A list of tools
Procedures to account for all employees after emergency evacuation has been completed
A list of visitors only
Procedures to account for all employees before evacuation starts, by checking the daily sign-in sheet at the trailer
test.explanation: The plan must include procedures to account for all employees after emergency evacuation has been completed (1926.35(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: foremen bring their daily sign-in sheets to the muster point.

test.question: Under 1926.50(e), what must be provided for an injured person?
options: A first aid kit, with the injured person waiting until the shift ends to be taken for care
A posted list of the nearest hospital and clinic phone numbers at the trailer, without any working phone, radio, or vehicle needing to be kept on site
Proper equipment for prompt transportation to a physician or hospital, or a communication system for contacting ambulance service
Only a stretcher
test.explanation: Proper equipment for prompt transportation of the injured person to a physician or hospital, or a communication system for contacting ambulance service, must be provided (1926.50(e)). Job-site scenario: a remote site keeps a vehicle and a satellite phone available for emergencies.

test.question: Under 1926.150(a)(2)-(3), what is required of firefighting equipment?
options: It must be kept in a locked job-site trailer, with the key held by the foreman or the fire watch
Only the foreman needs to know where it is
It must be stored out of sight in the tool crib to prevent theft
Access to it must be maintained at all times, and it must be conspicuously located
test.explanation: Access to all available firefighting equipment must be maintained at all times (1926.150(a)(2)), and employer-provided firefighting equipment must be conspicuously located (1926.150(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: extinguishers are not blocked by material deliveries and are marked with signs.

test.question: 1926.35(c)(1) requires an employee alarm system complying with 1926.159, which Appendix A to Part 1926 designates as 1910.165. Under 1910.165(b)(2), how must the alarm perform?
options: It must be audible above ambient noise at the site office and muster point, with crews in noisy work areas relying on a foreman or supervisor to relay the alarm to them by voice or two-way radio
It must be perceivable above ambient noise or light levels by all employees in affected areas (tactile devices may be used for employees who cannot recognize audible or visual alarms)
It must be a siren
It must be tested annually only
test.explanation: The employer must establish an employee alarm system that complies with 1926.159 (1926.35(c)(1)). Appendix A to Part 1926 designates 1926.159 as 1910.165, Employee alarm systems. Under that section, the alarm must be perceivable above ambient noise or light levels by all employees in the affected portions of the workplace, and tactile devices may be used for those who cannot recognize an audible or visual alarm (1910.165(b)(2)). It must also be distinctive and recognizable as a signal to evacuate or act under the plan (1910.165(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: on a noisy demolition floor, strobe lights are added to the air-horn evacuation signal.

title: Ionizing and Nonionizing Radiation
topics: Competent persons for radioactive materials and X-rays
Laser warning placards and beam control

resources.title: eCFR: 29 CFR 1926.54
resources.description: Current official text of the nonionizing radiation standard

test.question: Under 1926.53(a), which standards apply to construction activities using sources of ionizing radiation?
options: The pertinent provisions of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's Standards for Protection Against Radiation (10 CFR part 20)
OSHA's nonionizing radiation rules in 1926.54
The Department of Energy's radiation rules (10 CFR part 835), in place of the NRC's 10 CFR part 20 standards on all construction and demolition sites
The equipment manufacturer's operating manual, used in place of the NRC radiation rules whenever the work is done without an NRC license
test.explanation: In construction activities using sources of ionizing radiation, the pertinent NRC provisions (10 CFR part 20) on occupational radiation exposure apply (1926.53(a)). Job-site scenario: a radiography subcontractor X-raying pipe welds works under its NRC or agreement-state license rules.

test.question: Under 1926.53(b), who may perform activities involving radioactive materials or X-rays?
options: Any trained laborer
Competent persons specially trained in the proper and safe operation of the equipment
Only the GC
Anyone with a badge
test.explanation: Any activity involving radioactive materials or X-rays, licensed or not, must be performed by competent persons specially trained in the proper and safe operation of the equipment (1926.53(b)). Job-site scenario: only the certified radiographer operates the source camera; other trades stay out of the barricaded area.

test.question: Under 1926.54(a)-(b), who may install, adjust, and operate laser equipment?
options: Any survey crew member who has read the manufacturer's manual, with the qualification card kept on file in the site office
Only the owner
Only qualified and trained employees, who must carry proof of qualification at all times
Any employee over 21 who has operated survey lasers before, without proof of qualification carried on the job
test.explanation: Only qualified and trained employees may install, adjust, and operate laser equipment (1926.54(a)), and proof of the operator's qualification must be available and in the operator's possession at all times (1926.54(b)). Job-site scenario: the laser-level operator carries their qualification card.

test.question: Above what potential exposure to direct or reflected laser light does 1926.54(c) require antilaser eye protection?
options: 1 milliwatt (0.001 watts), as for Class 2 lasers
5 milliwatts (0.005 watts)
50 milliwatts (0.05 watts), direct beam only
1 watt (1,000 milliwatts), as for Class 4 lasers
test.explanation: Employees working where potential exposure to direct or reflected laser light exceeds 0.005 watts (5 milliwatts) must be provided antilaser eye protection as specified in Subpart E (1926.54(c)). Job-site scenario: crews near a high-power alignment laser get wavelength-rated goggles.

test.question: What does 1926.54(d)-(e) require in laser work areas?
options: Standard laser warning placards posted, and beam shutters or caps used (or the laser turned off) when transmission is not needed; turned off when left unattended for substantial periods
Placards only where the laser exceeds 5 milliwatts
Warning placards posted only at the laser instrument itself, beam caps used only on lasers rated above 5 milliwatts, and the laser left running when unattended over lunch but turned off overnight
Lasers must run continuously
test.explanation: Areas where lasers are used must be posted with standard laser warning placards (1926.54(d)). Beam shutters or caps must be used, or the laser turned off, when transmission is not needed, and the laser must be turned off when left unattended for a substantial period such as lunch, overnight, or shift change (1926.54(e)). Job-site scenario: the pipe laser is capped during the lunch break.

test.question: Under 1926.54(g), may a laser beam be directed at employees?
options: Yes, briefly
No
Yes, if under 5 mW
Yes, with goggles
test.explanation: The laser beam shall not be directed at employees (1926.54(g)). Job-site scenario: the rotating laser is set above head height (1926.54(k) recommends this when possible).

test.question: What does 1926.54(h) require when it is raining, snowing, dusty, or foggy?
options: Operation may continue if the beam is raised above head height
Only turn the laser brighter
Laser operation must be prohibited where practicable, and in any event employees must be kept out of range of the source and target area
Only wear raincoats
test.explanation: When it is raining or snowing, or there is dust or fog in the air, laser operation must be prohibited where practicable. In any event, employees must be kept out of range of the source and target area during such weather (1926.54(h)). Job-site scenario: the survey laser is shut down in dense fog.

test.question: Under 1926.54(i), what label must laser equipment bear?
options: The purchase date
The operator's name
No label
A label indicating maximum output
test.explanation: Laser equipment must bear a label indicating its maximum output (1926.54(i)). Job-site scenario: before use, the operator checks the output label to choose eye protection.

test.question: Under 1926.54(l), employees may not be exposed to microwave power densities above:
options: 1 milliwatt per square centimeter
10 milliwatts per square centimeter
100 milliwatts per square centimeter
1 watt per square centimeter
test.explanation: Employees may not be exposed to microwave power densities in excess of 10 milliwatts per square centimeter (1926.54(l)). Job-site scenario: riggers on a telecom tower stay out of the antenna's near field while it is transmitting.

test.question: Under 1926.54(j)(1), employees may not be exposed to direct-staring laser light intensities above:
options: 1 microwatt per square centimeter
1 milliwatt per square centimeter
2.5 watts per square centimeter
10 milliwatts per square centimeter
test.explanation: Employees may not be exposed to light intensities above 1 microwatt/cm2 for direct staring (1926.54(j)(1)), 1 milliwatt/cm2 for incidental observing (1926.54(j)(2)), or 2.5 watts/cm2 for diffused reflected light (1926.54(j)(3)). Job-site scenario: no one looks into the beam path of the alignment laser.

title: Stairways
topics: When a stairway or ladder is required

resources.title: Stairway and Ladder General Requirements
resources.description: When stairways or ladders are required

test.question: Under 1926.1051(a), when must a stairway or ladder be provided?
options: At every change in floor level of 12 inches or more, even where a ramp, runway, sloped embankment, or personnel hoist already provides safe personnel access between levels
At all personnel points of access with a break in elevation of 24 inches or more, where no ramp, runway, sloped embankment, mobile scaffold, or personnel hoist is provided
At all personnel points of access with a break in elevation of 19 inches or more, where no ramp, runway, sloped embankment, or personnel hoist is provided
Only in buildings over two stories
test.explanation: A stairway or ladder must be provided at all personnel points of access where there is a break in elevation of 19 inches or more and no ramp, runway, sloped embankment, or personnel hoist is provided (1926.1051(a)). Job-site scenario: a 24-inch step down from a slab edge to the footing needs a ladder or stair.

test.question: Under 1926.1051(a)(2), what is required when ladders are the only access for 25 or more employees, or serve two-way traffic?
options: A single ladder at least 24 inches wide, with a spotter at the base during shift changes
A rope ladder
One ladder plus a posted one-way traffic rule
A double-cleated ladder or two or more separate ladders
test.explanation: A double-cleated ladder or two or more separate ladders must be provided when ladders are the only means of access or exit from a work area for 25 or more employees, or when a ladder serves simultaneous two-way traffic (1926.1051(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: a job-built double-cleat ladder serves the 30-person deck crew.

test.question: A building has only one point of access between levels, and work will restrict it. What does 1926.1051(a)(3) require?
options: Keep it clear; if work restricts free passage, provide and use a second point of access
Keep it clear when possible; if work restricts free passage, post a flagger to sequence workers through the opening
Close the level
Post a sign only
test.explanation: With only one point of access between levels, it must be kept clear for free passage. When work or equipment restricts that passage, a second point of access must be provided and used (1926.1051(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: while the stair is being drywalled, a temporary ladder serves as the second access.

test.question: Under 1926.1052(a)(2), at what angle from horizontal must stairs be installed?
options: Between 20 and 40 degrees from horizontal
Between 30 and 50 degrees
Between 50 and 70 degrees from horizontal
Any angle
test.explanation: Stairs must be installed between 30 and 50 degrees from horizontal (1926.1052(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: a job-built stair to a mezzanine is framed at about 37 degrees.

test.question: Under 1926.1052(a)(3), how much may riser height or tread depth vary within a stairway system?
options: Up to 1 inch
Up to 1/2 inch
No more than 1/4 inch
Any amount
test.explanation: Riser height and tread depth must be uniform within each flight, including any foundation structure used as a tread, and variations may not exceed 1/4 inch in any stairway system (1926.1052(a)(3)). Job-site scenario: the bottom step onto an uneven slab is shimmed so it matches the others.

test.question: Under 1926.1052(a)(1), what landings must temporary stairways (not part of the permanent structure) have?
options: Landings only at floor levels, however far apart
Landings at least 24 inches in the direction of travel and at least 18 inches wide at every 20 feet or less of vertical rise, and at the top
Only at the top
Landings at least 30 inches in the direction of travel and at least 22 inches wide at every 12 feet or less of vertical rise
test.explanation: Stairways that will not be part of the permanent structure must have landings at least 30 inches in the direction of travel and at least 22 inches wide at every 12 feet or less of vertical rise (1926.1052(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: a temporary scaffold-stair to the roof has a landing every 12 feet.

test.question: Under 1926.1052(b)(1), may workers walk on metal pan stairs before the pans are filled with concrete?
options: No, except during stairway construction, unless the pans are temporarily filled with wood or other solid material at least to the top edge of each pan
Yes, always
Yes, if they wear boots
Only going down
test.explanation: Except during stairway construction, foot traffic is prohibited on pan stairs whose treads or landings will be filled later, unless the pans are temporarily fitted with wood or other solid material at least to the top edge of each pan (1926.1052(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: plywood inserts go into the pans before trades use the stair.

test.question: Under 1926.1052(c)(1), when must a stairway have at least one handrail and a stairrail system on each unprotected side?
options: When it has more than 10 risers or rises more than 6 feet, whichever is greater, on any open side
When it has four or more risers or rises more than 30 inches, whichever is less
When it has four or more risers or rises more than 48 inches, whichever is greater
Only once permanent treads are installed
test.explanation: Stairways with four or more risers, or rising more than 30 inches (whichever is less), must have at least one handrail and a stairrail system along each unprotected side or edge (1926.1052(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: a five-riser temporary stair to the trailer gets rails.

test.question: Under 1926.1052(c)(6), what is the required height range for handrails?
options: Not less than 24 inches nor more than 30 inches from the handrail top to the tread surface, measured at the back edge of the tread
Not less than 39 inches nor more than 45 inches from the handrail top to the tread surface, matching the 42-inch guardrail top rail
Not less than 30 inches nor more than 37 inches from the handrail top to the tread surface (in line with the riser face)
Not less than 38 inches nor more than 44 inches from the handrail top to the tread surface, measured at the nosing of each step
test.explanation: Handrails must be no more than 37 inches and no less than 30 inches from the upper surface of the handrail to the tread surface, measured in line with the face of the riser at the forward edge of the tread (1926.1052(c)(6)). Handrails and stairrail top rails must withstand 200 pounds (1926.1052(c)(5)). Job-site scenario: the handrail on the temporary stair is set at 34 inches.

test.question: Under 1926.1060(a)(1), who must train employees using ladders and stairways?
options: Anyone
The manufacturer only
A competent person, covering ladder inspection and load ratings only, once at hire
A competent person, covering fall hazards, fall protection procedures, proper construction and use of stairways and ladders, load capacities, and the Subpart X standards
test.explanation: The employer must ensure each employee using ladders and stairways is trained by a competent person, as applicable, in the nature of fall hazards, fall protection procedures, proper construction, use, placement, and care of stairways and ladders, ladder load capacities, and the Subpart X standards (1926.1060(a)(1)). Retraining is required as necessary (1926.1060(b)). Job-site scenario: new hires get stair and ladder training from the site competent person.

title: Working Over or Near Water and Safety Nets
topics: Life jackets and buoyant work vests

resources.title: Safety Net Systems
resources.description: Safety net criteria and practices under Subpart M

test.question: Under 1926.106(a), what must employees working over or near water, where the danger of drowning exists, be provided with?
options: U.S. Coast Guard-approved life jackets or buoyant work vests
Nothing, if each employee passes a swim test before starting work
Any commercially sold foam float or life ring, kept within reach of the work area
A rope only
test.explanation: Employees working over or near water where the danger of drowning exists must be provided with U.S. Coast Guard-approved life jackets or buoyant work vests (1926.106(a)). Job-site scenario: the bridge-deck form crew wears USCG-approved work vests.

test.question: Under 1926.106(b), when must buoyant work vests or life preservers be inspected?
options: Monthly
Prior to and after each use, and defective units may not be used
Annually
Only when new
test.explanation: Buoyant work vests or life preservers must be inspected before and after each use for defects that would alter their strength or buoyancy, and defective units may not be used (1926.106(b)). Job-site scenario: a vest with a torn shell is pulled from service.

test.question: Under 1926.106(c), how much line must ring buoys have?
options: At least 50 feet
At least 150 feet
At least 90 feet
Any length
test.explanation: Ring buoys with at least 90 feet of line must be provided and readily available for emergency rescue (1926.106(c)). Job-site scenario: each ring buoy on the pier has a 90-foot line coiled and ready.

test.question: Under 1926.106(c), what is the maximum distance between ring buoys?
options: 50 feet
200 feet
test.explanation: The distance between ring buoys may not exceed 200 feet (1926.106(c)). Job-site scenario: on a 600-foot wharf repair, at least four ring buoys are spaced along the work area.

test.question: Under 1926.106(d), what must be immediately available where employees work over or adjacent to water?
options: At least one lifesaving skiff
A diver
A helicopter
At least one ring buoy with 50 feet of line
test.explanation: At least one lifesaving skiff must be immediately available at locations where employees work over or adjacent to water (1926.106(d)). Job-site scenario: a manned skiff stands by below the bridge deck.

test.question: Under 1926.502(c)(2), when the net is more than 10 feet below the working level, how far must it extend outward from the outermost projection of the work surface?
options: 8 feet
10 feet
13 feet
20 feet
test.explanation: Safety nets must extend outward from the outermost projection of the work surface at least 8 feet when the net is up to 5 feet below, 10 feet when more than 5 up to 10 feet below, and 13 feet when more than 10 feet below (1926.502(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: a net hung 15 feet below a bridge deck edge must reach at least 13 feet out.

test.question: Under 1926.502(c)(4)(i), when must safety nets and their installations be drop-tested at the jobsite (unless the employer shows it is unreasonable and certifies the net instead)?
options: Only once, at the factory
Monthly with a 200-pound weight
After initial installation and before use, whenever relocated, after major repair, and at 6-month intervals if left in one place, using a 400-pound bag of sand 30 ±2 inches in diameter
Only after a fall or a dropped load lands in the net
test.explanation: Nets and installations must be drop-tested at the jobsite after initial installation and before use, whenever relocated, after major repair, and at 6-month intervals if left in place. The test uses a 400-pound bag of sand 30 ±2 inches in diameter (1926.502(c)(4)(i)). If the employer can show the drop test is unreasonable, the employer or a designated competent person must prepare a certification record instead before the net is used (1926.502(c)(4)(ii)). Job-site scenario: the net is drop-tested again after it is moved to the next bay.

test.question: Under 1926.502(c)(5), how often must safety nets be inspected?
options: At least once a month for wear, damage, and deterioration, and again after each relocation, repair, or drop test of the net system
Annually
Only after a fall
At least once a week for wear, damage, and deterioration, and after any occurrence that could affect the net's integrity
test.explanation: Safety nets must be inspected at least once a week for wear, damage, and other deterioration, and after any occurrence that could affect the integrity of the system. Defective nets may not be used, and defective components must be removed from service (1926.502(c)(5)). Job-site scenario: after a steel beam drops into the net, it is inspected before anyone works above it again.

test.question: Under 1926.502(c)(6), when must materials, scrap, equipment, and tools that fall into a safety net be removed?
options: As soon as possible, and at least before the next work shift
At the end of each work week, or sooner if debris covers more than a quarter of the net
Once debris builds up enough to sag the net below its required clearance
Only at project end
test.explanation: Materials, scrap pieces, equipment, and tools that have fallen into the safety net must be removed as soon as possible, and at least before the next work shift (1926.502(c)(6)). Job-site scenario: bolts and offcuts are cleared from the net at the end of each day.

test.question: Under 1926.502(c)(7), what is the maximum size of a safety net mesh opening?
options: No more than 64 square inches, and no side or center-to-center measurement of mesh ropes longer than 8 inches
No more than 36 square inches, and no side or center-to-center measurement longer than 6 inches
Any size, as long as the border rope has a 5,000-pound breaking strength
No more than 144 square inches, with each side no longer than 12 inches when measured center-to-center
test.explanation: Each mesh opening may not exceed 36 square inches or be longer than 6 inches on any side, and the opening measured center-to-center of mesh ropes or webbing may not exceed 6 inches. All mesh crossings must be secured against enlargement (1926.502(c)(7)). Border ropes must have at least 5,000 pounds breaking strength (1926.502(c)(8)). Job-site scenario: a net with 8-inch mesh is rejected.

title: Rollover Protective Structures and Overhead Protection

resources.title: ROPS Scope
resources.description: Which equipment must have rollover protective structures

resources.title: Overhead Protection for Tractors
resources.description: Overhead protection for agricultural and industrial tractors

test.question: Which equipment does Subpart W (1926.1000(a)) cover for rollover protective structures?
options: Only cranes
Only pickup trucks
Rubber-tired self-propelled scrapers, front-end loaders, dozers; wheel-type ag and industrial tractors; crawler tractors and loaders; motor graders; compactors and skid steers made after 7/15/2019

Rubber-tired self-propelled scrapers, front-end loaders, and dozers; crawler tractors; motor graders; sideboom pipelaying tractors; pre-2019 skid steers, but not wheel-type agricultural or industrial tractors
test.explanation: Subpart W applies to rubber-tired self-propelled scrapers, rubber-tired front-end loaders, rubber-tired dozers, wheel-type agricultural and industrial tractors, crawler tractors, crawler-type loaders, and motor graders used in construction. It also applies to compactors and rubber-tired skid-steer equipment manufactured after July 15, 2019, and does not apply to sideboom pipelaying tractors (1926.1000(a)). Job-site scenario: the crawler dozer on the grading job must have ROPS.

test.question: Under 1926.1000(b), what ROPS standard applies to covered equipment (other than compactors and skid steers) manufactured before July 15, 2019?
options: Only a falling object protective structure (FOPS) and operator seat belt, with ROPS optional on machines built before July 15, 2019
No ROPS at all, since machines built before July 15, 2019 are grandfathered as long as they have seat belts and a falling object guard
ROPS meeting ISO 5700:2013 for all covered equipment, since the SAE criteria in 1926.1001(b) no longer apply to machines built before 2019
ROPS meeting the minimum performance standards in 1926.1001(b) (and 1926.1002(b) for agricultural and industrial tractors)
test.explanation: Covered equipment (excluding compactors and rubber-tired skid steers) manufactured before July 15, 2019, must have ROPS meeting 1926.1001(b). Agricultural and industrial tractors must meet 1926.1002(b) (1926.1000(b)). Job-site scenario: an older loader's ROPS is checked against the SAE criteria referenced in 1926.1001(b).

test.question: Under 1926.1001(c), what must ROPS on the equipment listed in 1926.1001(a) (scrapers, loaders, dozers, crawler tractors and loaders, motor graders, compactors, and skid steers) manufactured on or after July 15, 2019, meet?
options: The test and performance requirements of ISO 3471:2008
SAE J320a only
No standard
Local codes only
test.explanation: For the equipment listed in 1926.1001(a) manufactured on or after July 15, 2019, ROPS must meet the test and performance requirements of ISO 3471:2008 (1926.1001(c)). Agricultural and industrial tractors are covered separately by 1926.1002(c). Job-site scenario: a new skid steer's ROPS label references ISO 3471.

test.question: Under 1926.1000(d), how must a removed ROPS be remounted?
options: With bolts or welding of any grade, as long as a competent person visually checks the mounting before use
With bolts or welding of equal or better quality than required for the original mounting
With bolts one grade lower than the original mounting bolts, or with tack welds, as long as the manufacturer's torque values are still followed
It need not be remounted
test.explanation: A ROPS removed for any reason must be remounted with bolts or welding of equal or better quality than required for the original mounting (1926.1000(d)). Job-site scenario: after a repair, the mechanic uses grade-matched bolts torqued to spec.

test.question: Which information must be permanently affixed to each ROPS under 1926.1000(e)?
options: The operator's name
The purchase price
The manufacturer or fabricator's name and address, the ROPS model number (if any), and the machine make, model, or series it is designed to fit
The last inspection date
test.explanation: Each ROPS must have permanently affixed the manufacturer or fabricator's name and address, the ROPS model number (if any), and the machine make, model, or series number it is designed to fit (1926.1000(e)(1)-(3)). Job-site scenario: a ROPS swapped from another machine is checked to confirm the label matches this model.

test.question: Under 1926.1002(e)(1), what is an "agricultural tractor" for Subpart W?
options: A wheel- or track-type vehicle of more than 50 engine horsepower, used in construction, designed to furnish power to pull, propel, or drive implements
Any crawler
A pickup truck
A wheel-type vehicle of more than 20 engine horsepower, used in construction, designed to furnish power to pull, propel, or drive implements
test.explanation: An agricultural tractor is a wheel-type vehicle of more than 20 engine horsepower, used in construction work, designed to furnish power to pull, propel, or drive implements (1926.1002(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: a farm-style tractor pulling a landscape rake on site is covered.

test.question: What does 1926.1003(a) say overhead protection on agricultural and industrial tractors is meant to protect against?
options: Injury from overhead objects such as flying or falling objects, and from the cover itself in an accidental upset
Injury from rollover only; it is not meant to protect against flying or falling objects striking the operator from above
Sun, rain, and heat exposure during long shifts, acting as a weather canopy rather than a guard against falling objects
Only dust
test.explanation: Overhead protection is meant to minimize operator injury from overhead objects, such as flying or falling objects, and from the cover itself in the event of an accidental upset (1926.1003(a)). Job-site scenario: a tractor working under trees during clearing has a rated canopy.

test.question: For machines also covered by 1926.604 (site clearing), what overhead protection does 1926.1003(d) allow?
options: Only the 1926.604 type, since site clearing rules override Subpart W
Either the type in 1926.604 or the type in 1926.1003
Any canopy rated by the dealer
Only a fully enclosed cab with a tested falling object guard
test.explanation: For machines covered by 1926.604 (site clearing), the overhead protection may be either the type provided in 1926.604 or the type provided in 1926.1003 (1926.1003(d)). Week 32 covers the 1926.604 canopy specifications. Job-site scenario: a clearing tractor with the 1926.604 mesh canopy meets the requirement.

test.question: Under 1926.1000(f), when is a machine with ROPS deemed in compliance even if not built to 1926.1001?
options: If its ROPS meets the State of Texas or local building code requirements
If the machine is less than 10 years old and its ROPS has been inspected and certified within the past 12 months by the equipment dealer, rental company, or insurer
If it meets the ROPS requirements of the State of California, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, or the Bureau of Reclamation in effect on the date specified
If it is less than 5 years old
test.explanation: A machine in use with ROPS is deemed in compliance if it meets the ROPS requirements of the State of California, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (EM-385-1-1, March 1967), or the Bureau of Reclamation, as in effect on the date specified in the paragraph (1926.1000(f)). Job-site scenario: an older federal-project dozer certified to the Corps requirement is accepted.

test.question: Under 1926.1002(e)(2), what is an "industrial tractor"?
options: Any forklift
A wheel-type tractor over 100 hp (including 1926.1001 rubber-tired loaders and dozers) for work such as landscaping, construction services, loading, digging, grounds keeping, and highway maintenance
Only road graders
A wheel-type tractor over 20 hp (not a 1926.1001 rubber-tired loader or dozer) for work such as landscaping, construction services, loading, digging, grounds keeping, and highway maintenance
test.explanation: An industrial tractor is a wheel-type tractor of more than 20 engine horsepower, other than the rubber-tired loaders and dozers in 1926.1001, used in operations such as landscaping, construction services, loading, digging, grounds keeping, and highway maintenance (1926.1002(e)(2)). Job-site scenario: a backhoe-loader tractor used for landscaping must have a qualifying ROPS.

title: Material and Personnel Hoists
topics: Personnel hoist door interlocks and stop switches

resources.title: Hoists and Elevators
resources.description: Material hoists, personnel hoists, and elevators

resources.title: Personnel Hoist Requirements
resources.description: Personnel hoist towers, cars, doors, and ropes

resources.title: Crane, Derrick and Hoist Safety
resources.description: OSHA overview of crane, derrick, and hoist safety

test.question: Under 1926.552(a)(2), what must be posted on hoist cars and platforms?
options: Rated load capacities, recommended operating speeds, and special hazard warnings or instructions
Nothing on the car itself; rated loads, speeds, and hazard warnings are kept in the operator's manual at the base of the tower
The owner's name, the hoist serial number, and the date of the last inspection, with load limits kept in the operator's manual
Rated load capacities and operating speeds, posted at the operator's station rather than on the cars and platforms
test.explanation: Rated load capacities, recommended operating speeds, and special hazard warnings or instructions must be posted on cars and platforms (1926.552(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: the material hoist platform shows "Capacity 3,000 lb - No Riders."

test.question: Under 1926.552(a)(3)(i), when must hoisting rope be removed from service for broken wires?
options: Three randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay, or two broken wires in any single strand within one rope lay
Six randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay, or three broken wires in one strand in one rope lay
Twelve randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay, or five broken wires in any single strand within one rope lay
Only when the rope parts
test.explanation: Hoisting rope must be removed when there are six randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay or three broken wires in one strand in one rope lay (1926.552(a)(3)(i)). Other removal criteria include heat or electrical damage and diameter reduction (1926.552(a)(3)(iii)-(iv)). Job-site scenario: the inspection finds three broken wires in one strand, so the rope is replaced.

test.question: What does 1926.552(a)(6) prohibit on construction sites?
options: All hoists
Elevators
Endless belt-type manlifts
Rack-and-pinion hoists
test.explanation: The use of endless belt-type manlifts in construction is prohibited (1926.552(a)(6)). Live booms on hoists are also prohibited (1926.552(a)(5)). Job-site scenario: an old belt manlift in a renovated plant is not used by construction crews.

test.question: Under 1926.552(b)(1)(ii), who may ride on a material hoist?
options: Anyone carrying materials
Only the operator
Supervisors and trained hoist operators, when no personnel hoist is available
No one, except for inspection and maintenance
test.explanation: No person may ride on material hoists except for inspection and maintenance (1926.552(b)(1)(ii)). Operating rules, including a "No Riders Allowed" notice, must be posted (1926.552(b)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: laborers send drywall up the material hoist and take the personnel hoist themselves.

test.question: Under 1926.552(b)(2)(i), how must hoistway entrance bars be placed?
options: At least 2x4 wood (or equivalent), 2 feet from the hoistway line, and 36 to 42 inches above the floor
At least 2x6 wood (or equivalent), 3 feet from the hoistway line, and 42 to 48 inches above the landing floor
At least 2x4 wood (or equivalent), flush with the hoistway line, and 30 to 36 inches above the floor, painted solid yellow
Optional
test.explanation: Hoistway entrances must be protected by substantial gates or bars painted with diagonal contrasting colors (1926.552(b)(2)). Bars must be at least 2- by 4-inch wood or equivalent, located 2 feet from the hoistway line, and 36 to 42 inches above the floor (1926.552(b)(2)(i)). Job-site scenario: striped bars across each landing stop workers from leaning into the hoistway.

test.question: What overhead protective covering does 1926.552(b)(3) require on material hoist cages or platforms?
options: 1-inch planking or 1/2-inch plywood
2-inch planking, 3/4-inch plywood, or other solid material of equivalent strength
Wire mesh only
A tarp
test.explanation: An overhead protective covering of 2-inch planking, 3/4-inch plywood, or other solid material of equivalent strength must be provided on top of every material hoist cage or platform (1926.552(b)(3)). The same applies to personnel hoists (1926.552(c)(7)). Job-site scenario: a plywood roof protects the hoist platform from falling debris.

test.question: Under 1926.552(b)(7), who must design material hoist towers?
options: The erection crew's competent person on site
The superintendent
A licensed professional engineer
The equipment rental yard
test.explanation: All material hoist towers must be designed by a licensed professional engineer (1926.552(b)(7)). Car arresting devices must function in case of rope failure (1926.552(b)(6)). Job-site scenario: the tower erection drawings carry a PE stamp.

test.question: Under 1926.552(c)(3), how often must personnel hoist towers be anchored to the structure?
options: Every 50 feet
Only at the top
Every 100 feet
At intervals not exceeding 25 feet, with a series of guys also installed
test.explanation: Personnel hoist towers must be anchored to the structure at intervals not exceeding 25 feet, and a series of guys must also be installed. Where tie-ins are not practical, the tower must be anchored by guys of wire rope at least 1/2 inch in diameter (1926.552(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: tie-ins are installed every 20 feet as the hoist mast climbs.

test.question: What does 1926.552(c)(8) require for personnel hoist doors and gates?
options: Electric contacts that prevent the hoist from moving when a door or gate is open
Padlocks
A warning bell that sounds when a door or gate is open, while still allowing the hoist to move
A sign reading "Close Gate Before Operating"
test.explanation: Doors or gates must have electric contacts that do not allow the hoist to move when a door or gate is open (1926.552(c)(8)). Job-site scenario: the hoist will not travel until the car gate closes and makes contact.

test.question: Under 1926.552(c)(13), what must be provided in a personnel hoist car?
options: An emergency stop switch at the bottom landing only
An emergency stop switch marked "Stop"
A first aid kit only
A fire extinguisher in place of a stop switch
test.explanation: An emergency stop switch must be provided in the car and marked "Stop" (1926.552(c)(13)). Normal and final terminal stopping devices are also required (1926.552(c)(12)). Job-site scenario: the operator shows new riders where the red Stop switch is.

title: Steel Erection: Controlled Decking Zones and Perimeter Protection
topics: Where a CDZ may be used

resources.title: Steel Erection Fall Protection
resources.description: Steel erection fall protection, including CDZs

resources.title: Steel Erection Training
resources.description: Training required for steel erection, including CDZ work

test.question: Under 1926.760(a)(2), when must perimeter safety cables be installed on multi-story structures?
options: At project completion
Only on the top floor
At the final interior and exterior perimeters of the floors as soon as the metal decking has been installed
Only if requested
test.explanation: On multi-story structures, perimeter safety cables must be installed at the final interior and exterior perimeters of the floors as soon as the metal decking has been installed (1926.760(a)(2)). They must meet the guardrail criteria in 1926.502 (1926.760(d)(3)). Job-site scenario: cables go up around the third-floor deck right after it is laid.

test.question: Under 1926.760(c), where may a controlled decking zone (CDZ) be established?
options: At any height
Only below 15 feet
Only on the roof
Over 15 and up to 30 feet above a lower level, where metal decking is initially being installed and forms the leading edge
test.explanation: A CDZ may be established in the area over 15 and up to 30 feet above a lower level where metal decking is initially being installed and forms the leading edge of a work area (1926.760(c)). Job-site scenario: decking at 24 feet uses a CDZ; at 35 feet it may not.

test.question: Under 1926.760(c)(1), from what fall hazards must each employee at the leading edge in a CDZ be protected?
options: Falls of more than two stories or 30 feet, whichever is less
Falls of more than 6 feet, the Subpart M threshold for leading-edge work
Falls of more than 15 feet above a lower level, the general steel erection trigger height
Falls of more than three stories or 40 feet, whichever is greater
test.explanation: Each employee working at the leading edge in a CDZ must be protected from fall hazards of more than two stories or 30 feet, whichever is less (1926.760(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: in a building with 12-foot floors, a decker at 26 feet (over two stories) must be protected.

test.question: Under 1926.760(c)(2)-(3), who may enter a CDZ, and how large may it be?
options: Any employee who wears a personal fall arrest system; boundaries marked with control lines or equivalent, no more than 90 feet wide and 90 feet deep from any leading edge
Only employees doing leading-edge work; boundaries clearly marked (control lines or equivalent) and no more than 90 feet wide and 90 feet deep from any leading edge
Employees doing leading-edge work plus the stud welders installing shear connectors behind them; boundaries marked with control lines, no more than 90 feet wide and 90 feet deep
Only employees doing leading-edge work; boundaries clearly marked with control lines or equivalent and no more than 3,000 square feet in area, measured back from the leading edge
test.explanation: Access to a CDZ is limited to employees doing leading-edge work (1926.760(c)(2)). Its boundaries must be designated and clearly marked with control lines or equivalent, and it may be no more than 90 feet wide and 90 feet deep from any leading edge (1926.760(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: control lines mark a 60 by 80 foot CDZ and the plumbers stay out.

test.question: Under 1926.760(c)(4), what must each employee working in a CDZ have completed?
options: Connector training under 1926.761
A first aid course
CDZ training in accordance with 1926.761
A crane operator certification
test.explanation: Each employee working in a CDZ must have completed CDZ training per 1926.761 (1926.760(c)(4)). Training must be given by a qualified person (1926.761(a)). Job-site scenario: only deckers with documented CDZ training are allowed past the control line.

test.question: Under 1926.760(c)(5), how much unsecured decking may be in a CDZ?
options: A 90-by-90-foot area
No more than 10,000 square feet
No more than one bundle
No more than 3,000 square feet
test.explanation: Unsecured decking in a CDZ may not exceed 3,000 square feet (1926.760(c)(5)). Job-site scenario: the crew secures sheets as they go so loose decking stays under 3,000 square feet.

test.question: Under 1926.760(c)(6)-(7), how must safety deck attachments be made in a CDZ?
options: From the leading edge back to the control line, with at least two attachments per metal decking panel; final deck attachments and shear connectors may not be installed in the CDZ
Anywhere, in any order
From the leading edge back to the control line, with at least one attachment per metal decking panel; final deck attachments and shear connectors are done inside the CDZ as decking advances
From the control line out toward the leading edge, with at least two attachments per metal decking panel; final deck attachments are made in the CDZ before the shear connectors are installed
test.explanation: Safety deck attachments must be made from the leading edge back to the control line, with at least two attachments for each panel (1926.760(c)(6)). Final deck attachments and shear connector installation may not be performed in the CDZ (1926.760(c)(7)). Job-site scenario: deckers tack each sheet twice; the stud welder waits until the area is outside the CDZ.

test.question: What criteria must perimeter safety cables meet under 1926.760(d)(3)?
options: Warning line criteria in 1926.502
The criteria for guardrail systems in 1926.502
Only the cable manufacturer's tensioning and anchorage instructions
The criteria for safety net systems in 1926.502, including drop testing
test.explanation: Perimeter safety cables must meet the criteria for guardrail systems in 1926.502 (1926.760(d)(3)), including top-edge height and 200-pound strength. Job-site scenario: perimeter cable is tensioned and checked for height and deflection like a guardrail.

test.question: Under 1926.760(d)(2), what may be used in a steel erection fall restraint system?
options: Body harnesses only, with positioning device components; body belts are prohibited in steel erection fall restraint systems
Rope tied around the waist
Either body belts or body harnesses, with fall arrest system components conforming to 1926.502
Body belts only, since harnesses are reserved for fall arrest
test.explanation: Fall arrest system components must be used in fall restraint systems and conform to 1926.502. Either body belts or body harnesses may be used in fall restraint systems (1926.760(d)(2)). Job-site scenario: a connector working near an edge uses a short restraint lanyard that keeps them from reaching it.

test.question: When may the steel erector's fall protection be left for other trades under 1926.760(e)?
options: Always
Only if the erector's foreman judges it safe

Only if the steel erector's competent person has inspected the cables and the nets, and the other trades' foremen have signed a written acceptance of control and responsibility before their crews work in the area
Only if the controlling contractor or its authorized representative directed the erector to leave it and inspected and accepted control and responsibility for it before other trades work in the area
test.explanation: Fall protection provided by the steel erector may remain for other trades only if the controlling contractor or its authorized representative has directed the erector to leave it in place (1926.760(e)(1)) and has inspected and accepted control and responsibility for it before authorizing others to work in the area (1926.760(e)(2)). Job-site scenario: the GC signs a turnover form for the perimeter cables before the curtain-wall crew starts.

title: Fall Protection Training
topics: Scaffold and steel erection training cross-references

resources.title: Fall Protection Topic Page
resources.description: OSHA fall protection overview and training resources

test.question: Under 1926.503(a)(1), which employees must receive fall protection training?
options: Each employee who might be exposed to fall hazards
Only employees assigned to work from personal fall arrest systems or on roofs
Only supervisors and competent persons who oversee elevated work
Only new hires
test.explanation: The employer must provide a training program for each employee who might be exposed to fall hazards, enabling them to recognize fall hazards and the procedures to minimize them (1926.503(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: laborers who occasionally work near slab edges are trained too, not just the roofers.

test.question: Which topic must fall protection training cover, as applicable, under 1926.503(a)(2)?
options: The selection, fit testing, and seal checking of respirators, plus hearing protection use and the written silica exposure control plan for crews working on elevated decks and low-sloped roofs
The use and operation of guardrails, personal fall arrest systems, safety nets, warning lines, safety monitoring systems, controlled access zones, and other protection to be used
Company history
The proper construction, use, placement, and care in handling of all stairways and ladders, the maximum intended load-carrying capacity of each ladder, and the ladder requirements of Subpart X
test.explanation: Training must cover, as applicable, the use and operation of guardrail systems, personal fall arrest systems, safety net systems, warning line systems, safety monitoring systems, controlled access zones, and other protection to be used (1926.503(a)(2)(iii)), among other listed topics. Job-site scenario: the roofing crew is trained on the warning line system they will use.

test.question: Under 1926.503(a)(2)(v), what must training cover for roofing work on low-sloped roofs?
options: The use of mechanical equipment on steep-sloped roofs only, since equipment limitations do not apply to low-sloped roofs
The shingle nailing pattern and the manufacturer's installation instructions for the roofing membrane
The limitations on the use of mechanical equipment during roofing work on low-sloped roofs
The installation of slide guards and roof brackets used to keep roofers from sliding off steep-sloped roof surfaces
test.explanation: Training must cover, as applicable, the limitations on using mechanical equipment during roofing work on low-sloped roofs (1926.503(a)(2)(v)). Job-site scenario: the crew learns why the warning line is set 10 feet back where the felt-laying machine travels toward the edge (1926.502(f)(1)(ii)).

test.question: Under 1926.503(a)(2)(iv) and (vii), training must also cover each employee's role in:
options: The company softball team
Payroll
Purchasing
The safety monitoring system (when used) and fall protection plans
test.explanation: Training must cover, as applicable, the role of each employee in the safety monitoring system when it is used (1926.503(a)(2)(iv)) and the role of employees in fall protection plans (1926.503(a)(2)(vii)). Job-site scenario: residential framers working under a fall protection plan are trained on their role in it.

test.question: What must the written fall protection training certification contain under 1926.503(b)(1)?
options: The name or other identity of the employee, the date(s) of training, and the signature of the trainer or the employer
Only the date
Only the trainer's phone number
The employee's name, the training topics covered, and the employee's signature acknowledging the training; no trainer or employer signature is needed
test.explanation: The employer must prepare a written certification record with the employee's name or other identity, the date(s) of training, and the signature of the person who conducted the training or of the employer (1926.503(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: the training roster is signed by the competent person who taught the class.

test.question: Under 1926.503(b)(2), which training certification must be maintained?
options: Any one past certification, kept on file for the duration of employment
The latest training certification
A sign-in sheet in place of a written certification
Only the original certification from initial hire
test.explanation: The latest training certification must be maintained (1926.503(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: after a refresher, the new certification replaces the old one in the file.

test.question: Under 1926.503(c)(1), which change requires retraining?
options: A change in lunch schedule
A change in the crew's foreman, even when the work and fall protection systems stay the same
Changes in the workplace that make previous training obsolete
A holiday
test.explanation: Retraining is required when changes in the workplace make previous training obsolete (1926.503(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: moving from flat-roof work to a steep-roof project with different hazards triggers retraining.

test.question: Under 1926.503(c)(2), when does a change in equipment require retraining?
options: Only at the annual refresher, regardless of equipment changes
Only when new harness colors arrive
Only when the new equipment comes from a different manufacturer, even if it is the same type of system used the same way
When changes in the types of fall protection systems or equipment to be used make previous training obsolete
test.explanation: Retraining is required when changes in the types of fall protection systems or equipment make previous training obsolete (1926.503(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: switching from guardrails to self-retracting lifelines requires retraining.

test.question: Under 1926.503(c)(3), a supervisor sees a worker tie off to a conduit. What does this require?
options: Retraining, because inadequacies in the employee's knowledge or use of fall protection show they have not retained the required understanding or skill
A written warning in the file, since retraining is needed only after a fall occurs
Only a verbal warning
A new harness
test.explanation: Retraining is required when inadequacies in an employee's knowledge or use of fall protection systems indicate they have not retained the required understanding or skill (1926.503(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: the worker is retrained on proper anchorage selection before returning to elevated work.

test.question: Under 1926.454(c), when must an employee who works on scaffolds be retrained?
options: Only at the employer's yearly refresher class, even when worksite changes or new scaffold types present a hazard they were not trained on, or their scaffold work shows clear inadequacies

When the employer has reason to believe the employee lacks the needed skill or understanding, including when worksite, scaffold, fall protection, or falling-object protection changes present a hazard they were not trained on, or their scaffold work shows inadequacies
Every month
Only after an injury
test.explanation: Scaffold retraining is required when the employer believes an employee lacks the needed skill or understanding, including where worksite changes (1926.454(c)(1)) or changes in scaffold, fall protection, falling-object protection, or other equipment (1926.454(c)(2)) present a hazard the employee was not previously trained on, or where inadequacies in the employee's scaffold work show proficiency was not retained (1926.454(c)(3)). Job-site scenario: a crew moving from frame to suspended scaffolds is retrained.

test.question: Before crane operations begin, how must the work zone be identified under 1926.1408(a)(1)?
options: It need not be
Only by the operator's memory
Either by demarcating boundaries (such as flags or a range limit device) and prohibiting operation past them, or by defining it as 360 degrees around the equipment up to its maximum working radius
Only on the lift plan
test.explanation: The employer must identify the work zone either by demarcating boundaries (such as flags or a range limit or range control warning device) and prohibiting operation past them (1926.1408(a)(1)(i)), or by defining it as 360 degrees around the equipment up to its maximum working radius (1926.1408(a)(1)(ii)). Job-site scenario: flags mark the swing limit on the side facing the street lines.

test.question: If the equipment could get within 20 feet of a power line, what is Option (1) under 1926.1408(a)(2)(i)?
options: Work faster
Determine the line's voltage and keep every part of the equipment, load line, and load outside the Table A minimum clearance distance
Keep the equipment, load line, and load at least 20 feet from the line by holding a planning meeting and erecting an elevated warning line
Confirm with the utility owner/operator that the line has been deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite
test.explanation: Option (1) is to confirm with the utility owner/operator that the power line has been deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite (1926.1408(a)(2)(i)). The other options are a 20-foot clearance (Option 2) or the Table A clearance (Option 3). Job-site scenario: the utility drops and grounds the line for the morning pick and confirms it to the crane contractor before work starts.

test.question: When encroachment precautions apply, what meeting does 1926.1408(b)(1) require?
options: A planning meeting with the operator and other workers in the area of the equipment or load to review the power line locations and the steps to prevent encroachment/electrocution
A pre-lift meeting with the employees to be hoisted, held before the trial lift
A meeting with OSHA
A planning meeting with the utility owner/operator and the controlling contractor's superintendent to review the line voltages and schedule deenergizing and grounding of the lines before the lift
test.explanation: A planning meeting must be held with the operator and other workers in the area of the equipment or load to review the power line locations and the steps that will prevent encroachment or electrocution (1926.1408(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: the morning huddle walks the crew through the flagged warning line.

test.question: Under 1926.1408(b)(2), what kind of tag lines must be used near power lines?
options: Steel aircraft cable
Non-conductive
Chain
Wire-core synthetic rope
test.explanation: If tag lines are used, they must be non-conductive (1926.1408(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: dry synthetic tag lines replace a wire-core rope.

test.question: Under 1926.1408(b)(3), where must the elevated warning line, barricade, or line of signs be placed when using Option (2)?
options: At 10 feet from the power line
At the property line
At 20 feet from the power line, in view of the operator, with flags or similar high-visibility markings
Anywhere on site
test.explanation: An elevated warning line, barricade, or line of signs, in view of the operator and with flags or similar high-visibility markings, must be erected at 20 feet from the power line under Option (2), or at the Table A distance under Option (3) (1926.1408(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: a flagged rope on stanchions marks the 20-foot line.

test.question: Under 1926.1408(b)(4), besides the planning meeting and warning line, what else must be done?
options: Only a second elevated warning line set 10 feet farther out than the first
At least one additional measure, such as a proximity alarm or a dedicated spotter, but only when the operator cannot see the elevated warning line from the operator's seat
Only lower the boom
At least one additional measure: a proximity alarm, a dedicated spotter, a range control warning device, a range-limiting device, or an insulating link/device
test.explanation: At least one of these must be implemented: a proximity alarm, a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with the operator, a device that warns the operator when to stop, a device that automatically limits range of movement, or an insulating link/device (1926.1408(b)(4)(i)-(v)). This does not apply to Subpart V work (1926.1408(b)(5)). Job-site scenario: a dedicated spotter with a painted ground line and radio watches the boom tip.

test.question: Under 1926.1408(c), when Option (3) is used, how quickly must the utility provide requested voltage information?
options: Within two working days of the employer's request
Within five business days of the employer's written request
Within one hour
No deadline; the utility responds as its schedule allows
test.explanation: Where Option (3) is used, the utility owner/operator must provide the requested voltage information within two working days of the employer's request (1926.1408(c)). Job-site scenario: the contractor requests voltages on Monday and receives them by Wednesday.

test.question: Under 1926.1408(d)(1), may any part of the crane or load be below a power line?
options: Yes, always
Not unless the utility has confirmed the line is deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite, except for the exceptions in (d)(2)
Yes, if the operator is careful
Yes, with a spotter
test.explanation: No part of the equipment, load line, or load may be below a power line unless the utility owner/operator has confirmed the line is deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite, except as provided in (d)(2) (1926.1408(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: setting trusses under a distribution line waits until the utility confirms deenergizing and grounding.

test.question: Under 1926.1408(e), how must power lines be treated?
options: As deenergized once a qualified electrician employed by the crane contractor tests the line with a voltage detector at the worksite and finds no voltage
As insulated
As energized, unless the utility owner/operator confirms the line has been and continues to be deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite
As the operator judges
test.explanation: The employer must assume all power lines are energized unless the utility owner/operator confirms the line has been and continues to be deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite (1926.1408(e)). Job-site scenario: an apparently abandoned line is treated as live until the utility confirms otherwise.

test.question: What must operators and crew be trained on under 1926.1408(g)(1)(i) about electrical contact?
options: Procedures after contact, including having crew members grab the load to steady it
Procedures after contact, including leaving the cab right away by climbing down the ladder while holding the handrails, then walking normally over to the crew
Procedures after contact, including touching the crane with the back of the hand to check for current before any crew member walks up to help the operator
Procedures after contact, including staying inside the cab unless there is imminent danger of fire, explosion, or other emergency requiring exit
test.explanation: Operators and crew must be trained on procedures for electrical contact, including the danger of touching equipment and ground at the same time, the importance of remaining inside the cab except for imminent danger of fire, explosion, or another emergency, the safest way to evacuate, step potential, crew staying clear of the equipment and load, and safe clearance distances (1926.1408(g)(1)(i)(A)-(F)). Job-site scenario: after a boom contacts a line, the operator stays in the cab and warns the crew away.

title: Injury and Illness Recordkeeping for Construction (Part 1904)
topics: What an establishment is in construction
Separate logs for projects lasting a year or more
Linking mobile employees to an establishment
Vehicle crashes in construction work zones

resources.title: Covered Employees
resources.description: Recording injuries to payroll, temporary, leased, and contractor employees

resources.title: Recordkeeping Policies and Procedures Manual (CPL 02-00-135)
resources.description: OSHA directive with guidance on construction work sites as establishments

test.question: Under 1904.46, for activities like construction where employees do not work at one physical location, what represents the "establishment"?
options: The main or branch offices, terminals, or stations that supervise the activities or are the base from which personnel carry them out
Each individual job site where crews report each day, with its own OSHA 300 Log kept on site even for jobs expected to last only a few weeks
The owner's office
The project owner's site office, since the owner controls the location where the construction work is physically performed each day on the project
test.explanation: For activities where employees do not work at a single physical location, such as construction, the establishment is represented by the main or branch offices, terminals, stations, etc. that supervise the activities or are the base from which personnel carry them out (1904.46 (definitions)). Job-site scenario: a contractor's short service jobs can be recorded under the branch office that dispatches the crews, or on a log covering short-term establishments (1904.30(b)(1)); either approach is permitted.

test.question: A general contractor treats its 18-month hospital project as its own establishment (OSHA's Recordkeeping Policies and Procedures Manual, CPL 02-00-135, treats construction work sites scheduled to continue a year or more as establishments). Under 1904.30(a), what is required?
options: Only listing the project's cases on the home office's 300 Log
