A separate OSHA 300 Log for that establishment, because it is expected to operate for one year or longer
A log only if there are over 50 workers
A log only for fatalities
test.explanation: A separate OSHA 300 Log must be kept for each establishment expected to be in operation for one year or longer (1904.30(a)). The regulation text defines construction establishments by the supervising office (1904.46); treating a construction work site scheduled to continue a year or more as its own establishment with a separate log comes from OSHA's Recordkeeping Policies and Procedures Manual (CPL 02-00-135) and the February 28, 2014 interpretation letter on 1904.30 (continuous presence at a job site for a year or longer). This is OSHA interpretation, not rule text. Job-site scenario: the 18-month hospital job gets its own 300 Log.

test.question: A contractor runs many jobs lasting a few weeks each. How may their injuries be recorded under 1904.30(b)(1)?
options: They are not recorded
On the 300 Log of the general contractor or owner whose site the crew is on, since a contractor's short-term jobs are not establishments for recordkeeping
On one OSHA 300 Log covering all short-term establishments (or logs covering short-term establishments for divisions or geographic regions)
Only on each injured worker's 301 Incident Report kept at the main office, since short-term jobs lasting under a year need no OSHA 300 Log at all
test.explanation: Records must still be kept for short-term establishments (those existing less than a year), but a separate log is not required for each. One log may cover all short-term establishments, or logs may cover short-term establishments by company division or geographic region (1904.30(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: all of a roofing contractor's two-week jobs share one short-term log.

test.question: Some employees float between job sites. Under 1904.30(b)(3), how are their cases recorded?
options: They are exempt
On any log the foreman chooses
Only on the 301
Each employee must be linked to one establishment, and the case is recorded on that establishment's log (or the log covering their short-term establishment)
test.explanation: Each employee must be linked to one of the employer's establishments for recordkeeping. The injury or illness is recorded on that establishment's 300 Log, or on a log covering the employee's short-term establishment (1904.30(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: a traveling estimator is assigned to the regional office's log.

test.question: An employee based at the main office is hurt while working at the company's 2-year highway project, which the company keeps as a separate establishment (per CPL 02-00-135, a construction site scheduled to continue a year or more). Under 1904.30(b)(4), where is the case recorded?
options: On the 300 Log of the establishment where the injury occurred (the highway project)
On the main office 300 Log, because that is the establishment where the employee normally works
On the state DOT's log, since the highway project sits on a public right-of-way owned by the state
Not recorded, because the employee was away from the establishment where they normally work
test.explanation: If the injury occurs at one of the employer's establishments, it must be recorded on the 300 Log of the establishment where it occurred (1904.30(b)(4)). The premise that the project is an establishment comes from OSHA's Recordkeeping Policies and Procedures Manual (CPL 02-00-135), not the rule text. Job-site scenario: the visiting superintendent's sprain goes on the highway project's log.

test.question: A contractor keeps all project logs at headquarters. What does 1904.30(b)(2)(i) require?
options: Each site must also keep a duplicate 300 Log
Central recordkeeping is allowed only if each injury's information can be sent from the site to the central location within 7 calendar days of learning that a recordable case occurred
Central recordkeeping is allowed only if the site mails a paper copy of its 300 Log to the central location each month, and the central office can return records within 30 days of any request
Only an annual transfer
test.explanation: Records may be kept centrally if the employer can transmit injury information from the establishment to the central location within seven calendar days of learning that a recordable case occurred (1904.30(b)(2)(i)), and produce records within the required time frames when asked (1904.30(b)(2)(ii)). Job-site scenario: the site safety lead emails each recordable case to the home office the same week.

test.question: Under 1904.31(a), whose injuries must an employer record?
options: All payroll employees (labor, hourly, salary, part-time, seasonal), but not executives, and not temporary agency workers whom the employer supervises day to day
Only union members
All payroll employees (labor, executive, hourly, salary, part-time, seasonal, migrant), plus non-payroll employees the employer supervises day to day
Only employees over 18
test.explanation: Employers must record recordable injuries and illnesses of all employees on their payroll, whether labor, executive, hourly, salary, part-time, seasonal, or migrant, and also of employees not on their payroll whom they supervise day to day (1904.31(a)). Job-site scenario: a seasonal laborer's recordable cut goes on the log.

test.question: A contractor uses laborers from a temporary staffing agency and directs their work daily. Under 1904.31(b)(2), who records their injuries?
options: The staffing agency always
Both the contractor and the agency, each on its own log
The workers themselves
The contractor, because it supervises them on a day-to-day basis
test.explanation: Injuries to employees from a temporary help service, employee leasing service, or personnel supply service must be recorded by the employer that supervises them day to day (1904.31(b)(2)). Job-site scenario: the GC's foreman directs the temp laborers, so the GC records their injuries.

test.question: On a multi-employer site, a drywall subcontractor's employee is injured. The sub's own foreman directs their work daily. Under 1904.31(b)(3), whose 300 Log does the case go on?
options: The subcontractor's, because the contractor's employee is under the contractor's day-to-day supervision
The general contractor's, because the injury happened on its project and the controlling contractor records all injuries on its site
The owner's
Both logs
test.explanation: If a contractor's employee is under the day-to-day supervision of the contractor, the contractor records the injury. If the host employer supervises that employee day to day, the host records it (1904.31(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: the drywall sub logs its own worker's injury, not the GC.

test.question: Under 1904.31(b)(4), must both the host employer and the staffing agency record the same temp worker's injury?
options: Yes; the staffing agency records it as employer of record, and the host records it too because the injury occurred at the host's site
No; they should coordinate so each case is recorded only once, on the log of the employer providing day-to-day supervision
Only the agency, since it is the employer of record that issues the paychecks, even when the host supervises the worker day to day
Neither
test.explanation: The host employer and the temporary help, leasing, or personnel supply service (or contractor) should coordinate so each injury is recorded only once, on the log of the employer providing day-to-day supervision (1904.31(b)(4)). Job-site scenario: the GC and the staffing agency agree in writing on who logs temp-worker injuries.

test.question: A self-employed electrician is injured on a contractor's site. Under 1904.31(b)(1), must the contractor record it?
options: Yes
Only if hospitalized
No; self-employed individuals are not covered by the OSH Act or Part 1904
Yes; the controlling contractor records injuries to everyone working on its site, including the self-employed
test.explanation: Self-employed individuals are not covered by the OSH Act or this regulation, so their injuries are not recorded (1904.31(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: an owner-operator electrician with no employees handles their own injury; it does not go on the GC's log.

test.question: A worker is hospitalized after a vehicle strikes them inside a highway construction work zone. Under 1904.39(b)(3), must it be reported to OSHA?
options: No; motor vehicle accidents on a public street or highway only have to be recorded on the 300 Log
Only if the vehicle that struck the worker was owned or driven by the employer
Only fatalities
Yes; motor vehicle accidents in a construction work zone must be reported
test.explanation: Motor vehicle accidents on a public street or highway generally need not be reported, but if the accident occurred in a construction work zone, the fatality, in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye must be reported (1904.39(b)(3)). In-patient hospitalization must be reported within 24 hours (1904.39(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: a flagger struck in the work zone and admitted to the hospital is reported within 24 hours.

resources.title: Hoisting Personnel
resources.description: Requirements for hoisting personnel with cranes and derricks

test.question: Under 1926.1431(d)(1), what is the maximum total load (platform, hook, load line, and rigging) when using a suspended personnel platform?
options: 75% of the rated capacity for the radius and configuration, except during proof testing at 125%
50% of the rated capacity for the radius and configuration, except during proof testing
100% of rated capacity
25% of rated capacity
test.explanation: The total load (with the platform loaded, including hook, load line, and rigging) must not exceed 50 percent of the rated capacity for the radius and configuration, except during proof testing (1926.1431(d)(1)). Job-site scenario: a crane rated 8,000 lb at the planned radius may carry no more than 4,000 lb total.

test.question: Under 1926.1431(e)(1), who must design the personnel platform and its attachment/suspension system?
options: The competent person who inspects the platform after the proof test
A qualified person familiar with structural design
Any welder
The rental company clerk
test.explanation: A qualified person familiar with structural design must design the personnel platform and the attachment/suspension system (1926.1431(e)(1)). Job-site scenario: a job-built basket is not used without a qualified designer's drawings.

test.question: Under 1926.1431(e)(4), what must the personnel platform itself (excluding guardrails and fall arrest anchorages) support?
options: Its rated load only
Its own weight plus at least twice the maximum intended load, without failure
Its own weight and at least five times the maximum intended load
At least ten times the maximum intended load, including its own weight
test.explanation: The platform itself, excluding the guardrail system and personal fall arrest anchorages, must support its own weight and at least five times the maximum intended load without failure (1926.1431(e)(4)). Job-site scenario: the manufacturer's data confirms a 5:1 design factor.

test.question: What must be posted on a personnel platform under 1926.1431(e)(12)?
options: The operator's name and the date of the last proof test
Only the owner's name
Only the color code
The platform weight and its rated capacity, on a plate or other permanent marking
test.explanation: The platform's weight and rated capacity must be conspicuously posted with a plate or other permanent marking (1926.1431(e)(12)). The platform may not be loaded beyond its rated capacity (1926.1431(f)(1)). Job-site scenario: the operator checks the plate before calculating total load.

test.question: Under 1926.1431(h)(1)-(2), when must a trial lift be made with the unoccupied platform?
options: Immediately before each shift in which personnel will be hoisted (and again when listed conditions change), loaded at least to the anticipated lift weight
Once per project
Only after an accident
Only once at each new jobsite, combined with the proof test
test.explanation: A trial lift with the unoccupied platform loaded at least to the anticipated lift weight must be made from ground level (or wherever employees will board) to each location the platform will be hoisted to (1926.1431(h)(1)). It must be done immediately before each shift in which personnel will be hoisted, and repeated in listed circumstances such as moving the equipment to a new location (1926.1431(h)(2)). Job-site scenario: each morning, the empty basket with test weights is flown through the route first.

test.question: Under 1926.1431(j)(1), to what level must the platform and rigging be proof tested at each jobsite?
options: 100% of the crane's rated capacity at the planned radius
125% of the platform's rated capacity
150% of the platform's rated capacity, held for 5 minutes
No proof test is needed if the manufacturer certified the platform
test.explanation: At each jobsite, before hoisting employees and after any repair or modification, the platform and rigging must be proof tested to 125 percent of the platform's rated capacity (1926.1431(j)(1)). Job-site scenario: test weights at 125% are held in the basket before anyone rides.

test.question: How must the personnel platform be hoisted under 1926.1431(k)(1)?
options: At normal working speed, slowing down only as the platform nears the landing
Using controlled free fall when lowering, and powered hoisting when raising
In a slow, controlled, cautious manner, with no sudden movements
At any speed
test.explanation: Hoisting of the personnel platform must be slow, controlled, and cautious, with no sudden movements of the equipment or the platform (1926.1431(k)(1)). Job-site scenario: the operator feathers the controls as the basket rises.

test.question: Under 1926.1431(k)(8)(i), what happens when wind speed (sustained or gusts) exceeds 20 mph at the platform?
options: Lifting continues normally
The lift is always cancelled
Only the operator decides
A qualified person must determine whether it is safe to lift personnel; if not, the lift must not begin or must be terminated
test.explanation: When wind speed, sustained or gusts, exceeds 20 mph at the platform, a qualified person must determine whether it is safe to lift personnel. If it is not, the lift must not begin, or must be terminated if under way (1926.1431(k)(8)(i)). Job-site scenario: with 25 mph gusts at height, the qualified person calls off the basket work.

test.question: What fall protection does 1926.1431(k)(10)(i) require for employees in the platform (except over water)?
options: A personal fall arrest system attached to a structural member within the personnel platform
None; the platform's guardrail system and grab rail meet Subpart M, so a personal fall arrest system is optional
A personal fall arrest system attached to the load line or crane hook above the platform's suspension system
A lanyard tied to the building
test.explanation: Except over water, employees in the platform must use a personal fall arrest system attached to a structural member within the platform. Over or near water, 1926.106 applies (1926.1431(k)(10)(i)). Job-site scenario: each rider clips to the basket's rated anchorage, not to the load line.

test.question: Under 1926.1431(m), who must attend the pre-lift meeting, and when?
options: The operator, signal person (if used), employees to be hoisted, and the person responsible for the task, held once at the start of the project, and not repeated for workers who join the crew afterward
The operator, signal person (if used), employees to be hoisted, and the person responsible for the task, before the trial lift at each new work location, repeated for newly assigned employees
Only the supervisor
Only the operator and signal person, at a daily tailgate meeting held after the trial lift
test.explanation: A pre-lift meeting must review the requirements and procedures (1926.1431(m)(1)). It must be attended by the operator, the signal person if used, the employees to be hoisted, and the person responsible for the task (1926.1431(m)(2)). It must be held before the trial lift at each new work location and repeated for newly assigned employees (1926.1431(m)(3)). Hoisting personnel within 20 feet of a line up to 350 kV is prohibited except for Subpart V work (1926.1431(n)). Job-site scenario: the pre-lift meeting is held at the crane before the first trial lift.

title: Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response (Construction)
topics: Site control and the buddy system

resources.title: HAZWOPER (Construction)
resources.description: Hazardous waste operations and emergency response

resources.title: HAZWOPER Training
resources.description: Training requirements for hazardous waste operations

resources.title: Hazardous Waste Topic Page
resources.description: OSHA overview of hazardous waste operations

test.question: Which operation is covered by 1926.65 under 1926.65(a)(1)?
options: Routine drywall installation
Painting an office
Clean-up operations required by a governmental body involving hazardous substances at uncontrolled hazardous waste sites (among the other listed operations, including emergency response to releases)
Pouring footings on a clean site
test.explanation: The standard covers listed operations, including government-required clean-ups at uncontrolled hazardous waste sites (1926.65(a)(1)(i)), RCRA corrective actions, voluntary clean-ups at recognized sites, TSD facility operations, and emergency response to releases or substantial threats of releases of hazardous substances (1926.65(a)(1)(v)). Job-site scenario: an excavation contractor hired for a Superfund soil removal is covered.

test.question: Under 1926.65(b)(1)(i), what must employers involved in hazardous waste operations develop?
options: A verbal plan
A written program kept at the corporate office that covers only emergency response, not the identification or evaluation of the site's safety and health hazards
An unwritten site safety plan explained at daily briefings, designed to identify, evaluate, and control safety and health hazards and to provide for emergency response
A written safety and health program designed to identify, evaluate, and control safety and health hazards and provide for emergency response
test.explanation: Employers must develop and implement a written safety and health program for employees in hazardous waste operations, designed to identify, evaluate, and control safety and health hazards and to provide for emergency response (1926.65(b)(1)(i)). Job-site scenario: the remediation contractor's site-specific HASP is on site and available.

test.question: Which item must a site control program include at minimum under 1926.65(d)(3)?
options: Use of a "buddy system", along with a site map, work zones, site communications, safe work practices, and identification of the nearest medical assistance
A site map, work zones, and site communications, with the buddy system used only for confined space entry and the nearest medical assistance left to the local fire department
Use of a "buddy system", a site map, work zones, and the nearest medical assistance, with site communications limited to a posted phone list and no emergency alerting means
A site map, work zones, site communications, and the use of a "buddy system", with medical surveillance exams taking the place of identifying the nearest medical assistance
test.explanation: The site control program must include at minimum a site map, site work zones, use of a buddy system, site communications including emergency alerting, standard operating procedures or safe work practices, and identification of the nearest medical assistance (1926.65(d)(3)). Job-site scenario: no one enters the exclusion zone without an assigned buddy.

test.question: What initial training does 1926.65(e)(3)(i) require for general site workers exposed or potentially exposed to hazardous substances?
options: 8 hours online
At least 40 hours of off-site instruction and at least three days of field experience under a trained, experienced supervisor
At least 24 hours of off-site instruction and at least one day of field experience under a trained, experienced supervisor, plus an annual 8-hour refresher
At least 40 hours of instruction, all of which may be completed as on-the-job field experience at the site, with no off-site classroom portion
test.explanation: General site workers such as equipment operators, general laborers, and supervisory personnel must receive at least 40 hours of off-site instruction and at least three days of actual field experience under the direct supervision of a trained, experienced supervisor (1926.65(e)(3)(i)). Job-site scenario: the excavator operator on the remediation job has a 40-hour HAZWOPER card and three supervised field days.

test.question: Under 1926.65(e)(3)(ii), what training do workers on site only occasionally for a specific limited task (such as surveying), and unlikely to be exposed over the limits, need?
options: At least 16 hours of off-site instruction and two days of field experience
40 hours and three days
At least 24 hours of off-site instruction and at least one day of supervised field experience
8 hours only
test.explanation: Workers on site only occasionally for a specific limited task, such as ground water monitoring or land surveying, who are unlikely to be exposed over the permissible and published limits, need at least 24 hours of off-site instruction and at least one day of actual field experience under direct supervision (1926.65(e)(3)(ii)). Job-site scenario: the survey crew has 24-hour training.

test.question: Under 1926.65(e)(4), what initial training do on-site managers and supervisors directly responsible for hazardous waste operations need?
options: 24 hours of initial training and one day of supervised field experience for every on-site supervisor, plus at least eight additional hours of specialized training at the time of their job assignment
8 hours
Only a supervisor certificate
40 hours initial training and 3 days supervised field experience (reducible to 24 hours/1 day only if supervising only (e)(3)(ii)-(iii) workers), plus at least 8 additional specialized hours
test.explanation: On-site managers and supervisors directly responsible for hazardous waste operations must receive 40 hours of initial training and three days of supervised field experience. This may be reduced to 24 hours and one day only if they supervise only employees under (e)(3)(ii) or (iii). They also need at least eight additional hours of specialized training on managing such operations (1926.65(e)(4)). Job-site scenario: the remediation superintendent holds the 40-hour card plus supervisor training.

test.question: Under 1926.65(e)(8), how much refresher training must covered employees, managers, and supervisors receive?
options: Eight hours annually
Four hours
40 hours annually
24 hours every three years
test.explanation: Employees covered by (e)(1), and managers and supervisors covered by (e)(4), must receive eight hours of refresher training annually (1926.65(e)(8)). Job-site scenario: the crew's 8-hour refresher is scheduled before their 40-hour anniversary.

test.question: Under 1926.65(f)(3)(i)(B), how often must medical examinations be made available to employees covered under 1926.65(f)(2)(i), (ii), and (iv)?
options: At least once every twenty-four months, unless the attending physician believes a longer interval (not greater than every five years) is appropriate
At least once every twelve months, unless the attending physician believes a longer interval (not greater than biennially) is appropriate
Only at hire
Only after exposure
test.explanation: Medical exams must be made available at least once every twelve months, unless the attending physician believes a longer interval, not greater than every two years, is appropriate (1926.65(f)(3)(i)(B)). Exams are also required before assignment (1926.65(f)(3)(i)(A)). Job-site scenario: remediation workers get annual HAZWOPER physicals.

test.question: Under 1926.65(q)(1), when must an emergency response plan for hazardous substance releases be developed?
options: After the first spill
Only if requested
Before emergency response operations begin; it must be written and available for inspection and copying by employees, their representatives, and OSHA
Within 30 days after the first emergency response operation; it may be kept verbally by the incident commander and described to OSHA personnel only on request
test.explanation: An emergency response plan must be developed and implemented to handle anticipated emergencies before emergency response operations begin. It must be in writing and available for inspection and copying by employees, their representatives, and OSHA personnel (1926.65(q)(1)). Employers who evacuate employees, do not permit them to assist, and provide an emergency action plan under 1926.35 are exempt from this plan requirement (1926.65(q)(1)). Job-site scenario: the contractor's written plan for a fuel tank rupture is in place before the work starts.

test.question: Under 1926.65(q)(6)(i), what does a first responder at the awareness level do?
options: Responds defensively to contain the release from a safe distance, keeping it from spreading and preventing exposures, after notifying authorities
Commands the incident
Performs decontamination of responders and equipment in the contamination reduction zone once the release has been stopped
Witnesses or discovers a release and initiates an emergency response sequence by notifying the proper authorities
test.explanation: First responders at the awareness level are individuals likely to witness or discover a hazardous substance release who have been trained to initiate an emergency response sequence by notifying the proper authorities (1926.65(q)(6)(i)). Job-site scenario: a laborer who smells gas from a struck line backs away and calls it in.

title: Arc Welding and Cutting
topics: Structures and pipelines as ground returns

resources.title: Arc Welding and Cutting
resources.description: Electrode holders, cables, grounding, operating instructions, and shielding

resources.title: Ventilation and Protection in Welding
resources.description: Ventilation and eye protection for welding, cutting, and heating

test.question: Under 1926.351(a)(1), what manual electrode holders may be used?
options: Only holders specifically designed for arc welding and cutting, with capacity to safely handle the maximum rated current the electrodes require
Any clamp-type holder that grips the rod firmly, as long as it is rated for the welding machine's maximum output and its jaws are wrapped with friction tape
Holders specifically designed for arc welding, rated for at least half the maximum current the electrodes require, since the welding arc is not continuous
Shop-fabricated holders made from a clamp and handle, if the grip and jaws are fully insulated with friction tape against the maximum voltage encountered to ground
test.explanation: Only manual electrode holders specifically designed for arc welding and cutting, with capacity to safely handle the maximum rated current required by the electrodes, may be used (1926.351(a)(1)). Job-site scenario: a cheap holder that overheats at the amperage needed for 1/4-inch rod is replaced with a properly rated one.

test.question: Under 1926.351(a)(2), which parts of an electrode holder must be fully insulated?
options: Only the handle grip, since the jaws must stay bare to hold the electrode
Current-carrying parts passing through the part the welder grips, and the outer surfaces of the jaws, insulated against the maximum voltage to ground
Only the cable
Only the jaw tips
test.explanation: Any current-carrying parts passing through the portion of the holder the welder grips, and the outer surfaces of the jaws, must be fully insulated against the maximum voltage encountered to ground (1926.351(a)(2)). Job-site scenario: a holder with cracked jaw insulation is taken out of service.

test.question: What type of cable does 1926.351(b)(1) require for arc welding and cutting?
options: Partially insulated, rigid cable sized to the welding machine's rated output, with bare sections allowed where the cable runs along the steel
Completely insulated, flexible cable sized to the machine's idle current only, without taking the duty cycle of the work into account
Completely insulated, flexible cable able to handle the maximum current of the work, considering the duty cycle
Solid wire
test.explanation: All arc welding and cutting cables must be completely insulated, flexible, and able to handle the maximum current requirements of the work, taking the duty cycle into account (1926.351(b)(1)). Job-site scenario: heavier leads are used for long runs at high duty cycle on structural steel.

test.question: Under 1926.351(b)(3), how must lengths of welding cable be connected?
options: Twisted together and taped
With hose clamps
With connectors of capacity at least equal to the cable; if lugs are used, they may be bolted together and left bare as long as they are kept up off the ground and away from the welder
With substantial insulated connectors of capacity at least equal to the cable; if lugs are used, they must be securely fastened with exposed metal completely insulated
test.explanation: Cable lengths must be joined with substantial insulated connectors of capacity at least equal to the cable. If cable lugs are used, they must be securely fastened for good electrical contact and the exposed metal parts completely insulated (1926.351(b)(3)). Job-site scenario: the crew uses rated insulated cable connectors to extend the lead up the column.

test.question: A welding cable (not the electrode-holder lead) is worn so bare conductors are exposed. What does 1926.351(b)(4) require?
options: The exposed portion must be protected with rubber and friction tape or equivalent insulation (cables in need of repair may not be used)
Keep using it as is
Wrap it in duct tape only
Throw it away at the end of the week
test.explanation: Cables in need of repair may not be used. When a cable, other than the electrode-holder lead covered by (b)(2), is worn so bare conductors are exposed, the exposed portion must be protected with rubber and friction tape or equivalent insulation (1926.351(b)(4)). Job-site scenario: a nicked section of the work lead is properly wrapped before use. Damage within 10 feet of the electrode-holder end is handled differently: that section may only have standard insulated connectors or splices of equal insulating quality, or it must be replaced (1926.351(b)(2)).

test.question: Under 1926.351(c)(1), what capacity must a ground return cable have when it serves more than one welding unit?
options: At least the specified maximum output capacity of the largest single welding unit that it services
At least the total specified maximum output capacities of all the units it serves
At least half the total specified maximum output, since the units rarely all weld at once
Any capacity
test.explanation: A ground return cable must have a safe current-carrying capacity equal to or exceeding the maximum output of the unit it serves. When one ground return serves more than one unit, its capacity must equal or exceed the total maximum output of all the units (1926.351(c)(1)). Job-site scenario: a shared ground for three 300-amp machines must be rated for 900 amps.

test.question: When a structure or pipeline is used as a ground return circuit, what does 1926.351(c)(3) require?
options: Clamp the ground lead near the work; joints along the structure need not be checked
Paint the joints
Confirm the required electrical contact exists at all joints; any arc, sparks, or heat at any point means the structure must be rejected as a ground circuit
Use it only at night
test.explanation: When a structure or pipeline is used as a ground return, it must be determined that the required electrical contact exists at all joints. Any arc, sparks, or heat at any point requires rejecting the structure as a ground circuit (1926.351(c)(3)). Pipelines carrying gases or flammable liquids may never be used (1926.351(c)(2)). Job-site scenario: sparking at a bolted splice means the welder runs a dedicated ground lead instead.

test.question: Under 1926.351(c)(4), what is required when a structure or pipeline is continuously used as a ground return circuit?
options: Bonding only the joint nearest the welding machine
An annual paint job
Joints need checking for electrical contact only once at setup; bonding and periodic inspections apply only to temporary ground clamps
All joints must be bonded, and periodic inspections must ensure no electrolysis or fire hazard exists
test.explanation: When a structure or pipeline is continuously employed as a ground return, all joints must be bonded and periodic inspections conducted to ensure no electrolysis or fire hazard exists (1926.351(c)(4)). Ground connections must also be inspected to ensure they are mechanically strong and electrically adequate (1926.351(c)(6)). Job-site scenario: on a long shop-fabrication run using the steel frame as ground, bonding jumpers are installed at each joint.

test.question: Under 1926.351(d)(3), what must the welder do when leaving the work for an appreciable time, or when the machine is to be moved?
options: Open the power supply switch to the equipment
Turn the output current down to its lowest setting and leave the switch on
Disconnect only the ground lead from the workpiece
Leave the switch on and coil the leads
test.explanation: When the arc welder or cutter leaves the work or stops for any appreciable length of time, or when the machine is to be moved, the power supply switch to the equipment must be opened (1926.351(d)(3)). Job-site scenario: before lunch and before dragging the machine to the next column, the welder kills the disconnect.

test.question: What does 1926.351(d)(4) require for faulty or defective arc welding equipment?
options: Repair it yourself and keep working without telling anyone
It must be reported to the supervisor
Report it only to OSHA
Return it to the manufacturer only
test.explanation: Employers must instruct employees that any faulty or defective equipment must be reported to the supervisor (1926.351(d)(4)). Job-site scenario: a welder notices the machine case is shocking and reports it before anyone else uses it.

title: Lift-Slab and Precast Construction
topics: Who may be in the building during jacking

resources.title: eCFR: 29 CFR 1926.705
resources.description: Current official text, including the non-mandatory appendix

test.question: Under 1926.705(a), who must design and plan lift-slab operations?
options: The general contractor's project superintendent, with plans that include detailed erection instructions, sketches, and provisions for lateral stability of the building during each lift
The competent person attending the manual leveling controls, with plans that include detailed erection instructions, sketches, and provisions for lateral stability of the structure during lifting
A registered professional engineer experienced in lift-slab construction, with plans that include detailed erection instructions, sketches, and provisions for lateral stability
The concrete supplier
test.explanation: Lift-slab operations must be designed and planned by a registered professional engineer experienced in lift-slab construction. The plans must include detailed instructions and sketches of the erection method and provisions for lateral stability during construction, and the employer must implement them (1926.705(a)). Job-site scenario: the lift sequence follows the PE's stamped jacking plan.

test.question: What does 1926.705(b)-(c) require for jacks and lifting units?
options: They must be marked with a rated capacity set by the jacking foreman
Only a daily visual check
Only paint-coded
They must be marked with the manufacturer's rated capacity and not loaded beyond it
test.explanation: Jacks/lifting units must be marked with their rated capacity as established by the manufacturer (1926.705(b)) and may not be loaded beyond that capacity (1926.705(c)). They must also be designed so they will not lift, or continue to lift, when overloaded (1926.705(e)). Job-site scenario: the crew checks each jack plate against the calculated column load.

test.question: Under 1926.705(d), what must jacking equipment be capable of supporting?
options: At least two and one-half times the load being lifted during jacking operations
The load being lifted
At least two times the load being lifted, with jacks never loaded beyond their rated capacity
At least five times the load being lifted, the factor used for all lifting hardware
test.explanation: Jacking equipment, including any load-bearing component used in the lifting operation, must support at least two and one-half times the load being lifted and may not be overloaded (1926.705(d)). Job-site scenario: lifting rods and nuts are rated for 2.5 times the slab load at each column.

test.question: Under 1926.705(g), how level must the slab be kept during lifting?
options: Within 2 inches
All support points within 1/2 inch of that needed to keep the slab level, with jacking synchronized
Within 1 inch
Level does not matter
test.explanation: Jacking operations must be synchronized for even, uniform lifting, and all support points must stay within 1/2 inch of that needed to keep the slab level (1926.705(g)). If leveling is automatic, a device must stop the operation when the 1/2-inch tolerance is exceeded or the system malfunctions (1926.705(h)). Job-site scenario: the control panel halts the lift when one corner drifts beyond tolerance.

test.question: If leveling is maintained manually, what does 1926.705(i) require?
options: Anyone may run the controls
Controls at each column
The controls must be in a central location and attended by a competent person experienced in the lifting operation and equipment while lifting is in progress
No attendant
test.explanation: Manual leveling controls must be in a central location and attended by a competent person while lifting is in progress. Beyond the 1926.32(f) definition, that person must be experienced in the lifting operation and the equipment used (1926.705(i)). Job-site scenario: an experienced lift-slab foreman stays at the central console for the whole lift.

test.question: Under 1926.705(j), what is the maximum number of manually controlled jacks/lifting units on one slab?
options: 16, if a competent person attends the controls
No fixed number, as long as a competent person attends the manual controls
test.explanation: The number of manually controlled jacks on one slab must allow the operator to keep the slab level within the (g) tolerance, and in no case may it exceed 14 (1926.705(j)). Job-site scenario: a slab needing 18 lift points uses automatic leveling instead of manual control.

test.question: Under 1926.705(k)(2), who may be immediately beneath a slab while it is being lifted?
options: No employee who is not essential to the jacking operation, under any circumstances
Anyone wearing a hard hat, once the slab has been raised above the height of the lifting collars
Workers from other trades, once the slab has been lifted more than halfway to its final level
Any employee, once an independent registered professional engineer has determined the building is reinforced sufficiently
test.explanation: Under no circumstances may an employee who is not essential to the jacking operation be immediately beneath a slab while it is being lifted (1926.705(k)(2)). Nonessential employees may not be in the building during jacking unless it has been reinforced as defined in 1926.705(k)(1), which requires a determination by an independent registered professional engineer. Job-site scenario: the electricians wait outside until the slab is secured.

test.question: When making temporary connections to support slabs, what does 1926.705(l) require?
options: Wedges may be loose
Wedges must be secured by tack welding or an equivalent method, and lifting rods may not be released until the wedges at that column are secured
Only one wedge per column
Wedges may be secured by tack welding or an equivalent method after the lifting rods at that column are released and the slab load settles onto the wedges
test.explanation: Wedges must be secured by tack welding or an equivalent method to keep them from falling out of position, and lifting rods may not be released until the wedges at that column have been secured (1926.705(l)). Job-site scenario: the welder tacks every wedge before the jack crew backs off the rods.

test.question: Under 1926.705(m)-(n), what applies to welding on lift-slab connections?
options: Temporary connections may be welded by any experienced ironworker, only permanent ones need a certified welder, and load may go to the columns once the shear plate welds are done, even while still hot
Only tack welds are needed
Only a certified welder familiar with the plan's welding requirements may weld temporary and permanent connections; no load transfer to columns until shear plate welds cool to air temperature
Load may be transferred to the columns once the welds stop glowing
test.explanation: All welding on temporary and permanent connections must be performed by a certified welder familiar with the welding requirements in the lift-slab plans and specifications (1926.705(m)). Load transfer from jacks to building columns may not occur until the welds on the column shear plates (weld blocks) have cooled to air temperature (1926.705(n)). Job-site scenario: the crew waits for the weld blocks to cool before releasing the jacks.

test.question: Under 1926.704(a), how must precast concrete wall units, structural framing, and tilt-up panels be handled until permanent connections are completed?
options: They may stand unbraced
Only braced overnight
They must be supported until temporary connections are made, and then the braces can be removed
They must be adequately supported to prevent overturning and collapse
test.explanation: Precast concrete wall units, structural framing, and tilt-up wall panels must be adequately supported to prevent overturning and collapse until permanent connections are completed (1926.704(a)). Lifting insert and hardware strength rules are covered in Week 24. Job-site scenario: tilt-up panels stay on pipe braces until the roof diaphragm is connected.
